speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I bring to the attention of the House yet another example of misplaced priorities in Government spending. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is quoted as saying that thousands of impoverished elderly Canadians need at least another $25 a month to live on, but the federal Government just cannot afford to give it to them.
When the entertainment bill of this Government is $10 million per year, when $60 million is budgeted each year to translate documents, when Canadian Unity advertising is $3.5 million, I resent being told that we cannot afford to help out the people who built this country. Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski):
That the Government re-examine its spending priorities with a view to eliminating waste and redirecting funds to areas where they are desperately needed.

Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of importance. Over 75 per cent of the voters in 78 Ontario municipalities added their voices yesterday to earlier similar local expressions in four other Provinces and approved Operation Dismantle-promoted disarmament referenda, urging the federal Government to pursue actively new international initiatives designed to speed the pursuit of balanced general and nuclear disarmament. Their message is clear-now is the time for our politicians to act. I therefore move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young):
That this House, acting in response to the demands of the people as expressed by way of referendum vote, call on the Government of Canada to review its position immediately and press, in the United Nations and elsewhere, to urge the holding of a global referendum on general and nuclear disarmament as a first step in promoting a renewed and vigorous race for peace.

November 9, 1982

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT OF FAMILY ALLOWANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, extensive debate is now prevalent on the universality of the Family Allowance Program. Governments are reluctant-in fact they lack the courage-to tamper with the universality of social programs because of the political consequences. Nevertheless, it is single and widowed women in our society who suffer most because they represent by far the largest group of unemployed as well as those most in need of upgrading their skills. Therefore I move:
That the Government establish immediately a system whereby mothers now receiving family allowance cheques can voluntarily opt out from this social program provided that the moneys so saved are placed into a fund which is used exclusively for generating jobs and for upgrading the skills of single and widowed women.
I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) would like to second this motion, as would many Members of the Liberal Party, Tory Party and the N.D.P.
November 9, 1982

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. The minister is aware that unemployment in Quebec has now reached alarming levels, and that Quebecair, a company that has been a transport carrier for thirty-five years, is represented here on Parliament Hill today, to ask the Minister of Transport whether he intends to make any proposals to save the company from bankruptcy. For a number of reasons, today, on behalf of the people from Quebec who are concerned about the unemployment rate in that province and who are afraid that 600 additional jobs will be lost, I wish to ask the minister whether he intends to bring this to the Cabinet's attention as soon as possible in order to try and find a way to safeguard the future of this carrier, a company that is very important to us in Quebec.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Quebecair employees who were on the Hill today expressed their views and their concern, and they said clearly that they did not want this to become a political issue. 1 must say I agree with them on all counts. One of the Hon. Members on this side of the House presented a motion under Standing Order 43 which would have received the consent of the House if the official opposition had supported it, but in any case, Madam Speaker, I can inform the House that Cabinet met this morning and ruled that in accordance with Clause 6 of Bill S-31, Quebecair would be exempted from the provisions of this bill as soon as they take effect.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER MINISTER INTENDS TO MEET QUEBEC COUNTERPART TO DISCUSS QUEBECAIR DIFFICULTIES
INQUIRY WHETHER MINISTER INTENDS TO MEET QUEBEC COUNTERPART TO DISCUSS QUEBECAIR DIFFICULTIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, you will agree that my question is very relevant. Therefore, considering the answer given by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, I would like to ask the Minister of Transport himself whether he intends to meet his Quebec counterpart with a view to finding ways of enabling Quebecair to operate in a sufficiently wide area to ensure its viability.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER MINISTER INTENDS TO MEET QUEBEC COUNTERPART TO DISCUSS QUEBECAIR DIFFICULTIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a decision just announced by my colleague proves that Bill S-31 was not aimed against Quebecair and I think that should be quite clear now. The next step, as the member for Joliette said, is to sit down and see whether a merger cannot be arranged between Quebecair and Nordair, something that has been discussed for a number of years. Now that the parties are aware of all the problems involved, there is a
possibility that they will approach the matter more realistically than they have done in the past. I hope so, and I have invited my colleague at the Quebec Department of Transport to a meeting within the next few days in order to discuss the fundamentals of this case.

subtopic: SUGGESTION THAT PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF NORDAIR AND QUEBECAIR BE RESTUDIED
SUGGESTION THAT PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF NORDAIR AND QUEBECAIR BE RESTUDIED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Minister of Transport has told us that he will be meeting with his Quebec counterpart, so perhaps the minister could inform the House whether he is also willing to reassess the proposal made on August 9 which mentioned Ontario and Quebec mergers with respect to Nordair. Could this proposal, which was rejected in August, be put on the agenda again for study and appropriate action?

subtopic: SUGGESTION THAT PROPOSED AMALGAMATION OF NORDAIR AND QUEBECAIR BE RESTUDIED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have already answered that question, and I explained that the Snow-Clair proposal had not been received very enthusiastically by the various parties involved. First of all, Air Canada was to participate in the merger, but without voting rights, a condition that Air Canada did not find very attractive. On the other hand, Nordair employees were not very enthusiastic either, and furthermore, parties from the private sector in Quebec and Ontario were, it seemed to me, either not very willing or not able to make substantial investments in the company that would be created as a result of a merger. In other words, a great many people did not seem to find the Clair-Snow plan very attractive, and I therefore hope that we shall be able to take a more realistic approach, for instance, in discussing Air Canada's participation in the merger, as a voting participant and not as a participant who provides funds without having a say in how they are spent.

Madam Speaker, I was interested in the Minister's reply to my colleague. The Snow-Clair proposal involved private funds, and I do not understand the Minister saying that is was not received positively by private interests in Ontario and Quebec, since that was the whole basis of the proposal. If the minister has disregarded the Snow-Clair proposal to resolve this contentious issue, when is he going to make up his mind on domestic air carrier policy, on which a unanimous all-party report of the Standing Committee on Transport was tabled in this House last spring, which made recommendations which might resolve this issue?

Madam Speaker, there is no relationship between the Quebecair
November 9, 1982

problem and domestic air carrier policy. I have studied its recommendations on domestic air policy and I will be in a position in the next few weeks to react to the very important suggestions made by the Standing Committee on Transport.
We do not need a transport system anyway.

Madam Speaker, a colleague behind me asks if we need a transportation system anyway. We certainly have a Minister of Transport who is almost utilizing his office against not just the committee but also against the CTC.

Madam Speaker, now that the Liberal Convention is over, and the Minister must have talked to some good Liberals around Ottawa over the weekend, when is he going to nominate someone as chairman of the CTC so that at least the CTC can get back into transportation and not have the Minister running the whole show?
Madam Speaker, my recommendations have already been sent to cabinet. If everything goes well, s'il n'y a pas de pepins, we should know the answer in about 15 days.

subsubtopic: CF-I8 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT-U.S. CONGRESSIONAL COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. We have just learned that Canada's new "Star Wars" fighter aircraft has flunked another performance test for the U.S. Navy. Not only that, but the U.S. House of Representatives Defence Appropriations Subcommittee reported that, in its opinion, the F-18 failed as a multi-mission aircraft because it is inadequate in its attack role.
In light of the F-18's poor report card and the fact that 70 per cent of Canada's planes are intended as attack planes, is the Minister still convinced that Canada's new $5.2 billion warplane is a good buy for the Canadian Armed Forces?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: CF-I8 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT-U.S. CONGRESSIONAL COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is not the first time that the F-18 has come under attack, and it has always won up until now. As for the Hon. Member's question, I think the article in the media today is like the articles we have seen on the CF-18 over the last three or four years. I think he knows very well that this report is related to the performance of the CF-18 during tests of landing on aircraft carriers. I can reassure the Hon. Member that we do not intend to buy an aircraft carrier. As far as the
Oral Questions
CF-18's that we have purchased are concerned, and the role that we bought them for, I can tell the Hon. Members that they are performing very well in tests at Cold Lake, much beyond the initial performance we expected from them on the last tests we had at Cold Lake.

subsubtopic: CF-I8 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT-U.S. CONGRESSIONAL COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, one role of the F-18 is to serve as an attack fighter in Europe. The report of the United States Subcommittee has pointed out that it is inadequate as an attack plane. The minister has avoided that part of my question.

subtopic: CHARGE THAT PERFORMANCE TEST WAS RIGGED
CHARGE THAT PERFORMANCE TEST WAS RIGGED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Minister is, of course, also aware that the U.S. Defense Appropriations Subcommittee has charged that an important performance test was rigged by either McDonnell Douglas or the U.S. Navy, in order to cover up the F-18's limitations. Was the Minister aware of this rigged test, and will he now reevaluate his decision to buy this high-tech lemon, before we sink any further into this quagmire?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: CHARGE THAT PERFORMANCE TEST WAS RIGGED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. When I receive the first test results, I can promise the Hon. Member that I will make it them public and he will then see that he is absolutely wrong about the CF-18.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FIVE CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. Government Ministers have announced five badly needed, major construction projects for New Brunswick. They are a zinc smelter to be located in Belledune; a large correctional institution in Renous; a new divisional headquarters for the RCMP in Fredericton; a military training facility in Oromocto, and DND pay directorate for Chatham. Not one contract has been let for any of these projects.
May I ask the Acting Prime Minister if he will co-ordinate and expedite measures to bring forward these projects which his Ministers say are necessary and important, so that New Brunswickers can obtain badly needed work in the construction trades this winter? Is the Acting Prime Minister aware

November 9, 1982
Oral Questions
that, in some areas where these projects are to take place, 40 per cent of the labour force is unemployed, and does he care?

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF FIVE CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS IN NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I could have named a couple of other projects in the same region, one of them being the Newcastle-Chatham port development, in my own Department. I know what I am doing with that particular project and I will inform my hon. friend about it, if he wants to know. All the other projects fall under other Departments. There will be a meeting of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs in a few minutes. I will bring this matter to the attention of my colleagues and deliver a collective answer to my friend as soon as I can.

Madam Speaker, 1 thank the Acting Prime Minsiter for his answers. I would draw to his attention the fact that the New Brunswick representative in the Cabinet has been removed from that Committee, and that is why I would ask him to pay particular attention to scheduling and co-ordinating these projects so that we can have work in New Brunswick that is desperately needed this winter, next winter, the winter after, and the winter after that. I am asking the Acting Prime Minister if he is going to give leadership to this country, or is he just going to pass the buck to another committee.

Madam Speaker, I presume that when my friend says "he" he refers to the Minister from New Brunswick. I can emphatically deny what the Hon. Member has just said. Only two or three days ago I had the Minister responsible for New Brunswick in my office at four o'clock in the afternoon. For a good period of time we discussed the particular issue I mentioned a moment ago, that is, the port facilities at Newcastle and Chatham. speechtext:
The reasons Elevator 1 at the Port of Montreal is being abandoned are twofold. The second reason is the development of what is referred to as-le projet du vieux port de Montreal-
-an organization which is very anxious to take hold of that land. I said at the time, and I repeat now, that there are other facilities available to Quebec farmers who want to deliver their grain by truck. They can go to Sorel, to Quebec City, and also to Trois-Rivieres.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister why he did not say what new facilities would be given in place of Terminal 1. The Minister must be aware that on May 28, 1982, Allstate Grain Company made an offer to purchase that terminal and continue to operate it as a grain terminal, and that his Government refused it. Madam Speaker, Montrealers are interested in the beauty of their city. That is why they look favourably on the development of the Vieux Port de Montreal. On the subject of elevator facilities, my hon. friend should know that an elevator has been built, Elevator 4. The problem is that Elevator 4 is not equipped to receive deliveries by truck. The reason is that the total export of grains in the Province of Quebec is 100,000 tonnes compared to the transfer capacity at the Port of Montreal of 8.1 million tonnes. It is therefore not judged to be necessary to spend $3 million in order to build that facility at Elevator 4.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Did he say no to the fact that this is the sixth anniversary of the establishment of the Ukrainian Public Group to promote-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PAPROSK1-S O. 43 MOTION OF MR. FLIS
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Member has to take my word that an Hon. Member of the House or some Hon. Members of the House said no. Therefore, the motion has to be considered as having been dealt with by the House.

The House resumed, from Wednesday, February 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres that Bill C-90, to amend the Customs Tariff and to repeal certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Madam Speaker, we must not let this Bill pass without bringing to the attention of Hon. Members certain provisions in the Bill that I am sure, if they knew their true import, they would be more than anxious to debate and have discussed on the floor of the House of Commons. I refer, of course, to Clause 5 of the Bill, which sets out certain provisions which would permit the Government by Order in Council to make changes from Imperial measurement to metric. This provision I suggest has in effect been snuck into this Bill without too much comment. It has far-reaching consequences and could have far-reaching, disastrous consequences for many businesses, industries and manufacturers in this country.
When you read the provisions set out, you see how underhanded the Government is in its approach to metrication in this country. Instead of approaching that question in a wholesome, above-board way, it has always tended to hide behind some type of Cabinet or Order in Council process to force metrication on Canadian business, industry and other Canadian activities.
I will have a second point a little later concerning Bill C-90, but I rise at this point with respect to Clause 5 because I believe the House of Commons must call a halt to the Government's propensity to rule by Order in Council. We in Canada are in a near depression, if not a depression, aggravated by faulty policies on the part of this Government. We must not allow the Government intentionally or inadvertently further to
complicate the already unsatisfactory economic conditions in which we in Canada find ourselves.
The world is clamouring for international business and activity. The United States of America, the wealthiest and most powerful nation in the world, is finding it difficult to tear itself from the depths of the recession in which they find themselves. We, on the other hand, are having a Bill introduced into this House that will have the effect of extending metrication even further than its present implementation in this country.
I refer to this in the context of the United States because, as we know, the metrication process has virtually been brought to a halt. Weighing the consequences of metrication, they decided they had trouble enough extracting themselves from the present recession without loading on to business a further complication and cost-destruction, if you like-by forcing business to accept metrication. As we know, President Reagan has commented that the metric commission in the United States has walked its last kilometer.
Is it not strange, then, that Clause 5 of Bill C-90 intends to take all of those items referred to in the Customs Tariff legislation and give the Cabinet of the day the power to change all Imperial measurements, the traditional British system which we have, unilaterally and without further reference to this House, with the obvious costs and difficulties for Canadian businesses and all who will use metrication in this country. I say that, Mr. Speaker, because I believe that if Hon. Members on both sides of the House read that provision, and thought of the consequences of it, they would, if not join in the debate, at least ensure that there will be careful consideration of the legislation in Committee of the Whole stage before it is passed by this House.
I know there are other Hon. Members who may want to speak on the impact of metrication in Canada. They may want to warn the Government in a more specific way what the fallout may well be if this clause is allowed to pass as part of Bill C-90. If the Hon. Members of this House believe that metrication in Canada has gone too far, has already aggravated in many ways the recession that we find ourselves in, and has in short brought on economic disturbance, annoyance, and in some cases even hardship at the retail levels, I suggest that they should not become a party to this Bill and allow it to be lightly passed.
I feel a second aspect of this Bill should be commented on, Mr. Speaker, which is the reference in many parts of Bill C-90 to an agreement with respect to trade between New Zealand and Canada. I draw Hon. Members' attention to these references because I feel this is somewhat of a precedent. If you read the notice of the Ways and Means motion which was brought in on November 12, 1981 it in no way indicates that the Bill has anything to do with any agreement with respect to
November 9, 1982

trade or any other particular arrangement with New Zealand. In fact, the explanatory note on page la of Bill C-90 simply says, and I quote:
This Bill would implement the Ways and Means Motion relating to the Customs Tariff that was tabled by the Minister of Finance on November 12, 1981.
There is no indication or notice that somehow or other, couched in that Bill, is an agreement, and references to an agreement, with respect to trade between New Zealand and Canada.
I am referring partly to a question of form. I believe that we, as Members, must always be very much on the alert for a Government that tends to smuggle pieces of legislation, references to agreements, in a Bill that you would never normally expect such agreements to be found in. When we are considering the question of what kind of ongoing arrangement we should have with New Zealand, country to country, if parliamentary approval is required there should at least be fair notice to all Members of this House concerning what they are being asked to approve. Above all, it should not be something that merely gets tucked into another Bill without due notice of the implications, and how far-reaching an effect it may have.
I say this in particular with respect to New Zealand because Hon. Members will remember that this Government was totally lax in its attention to detail a few years ago and allowed a wrinkle to be pulled wherein the Canadian public put up $50 million in the form of preferred shares which went into a Canadian entity, which then had a capital of $100,000. The $50 million was, if you like, the subscribed cost of preferred shares in the New Zealand Shipping Corporation (Canada) Limited. The point I would like to make, Mr. Speaker, is that until attention was drawn to this deal, the Government was unaware of the fact that what had transpired was that the New Zealand government, through a Crown corporation called the New Zealand Shipping Corporation, had set up a subsidiary in Canada known as New Zealand Shipping Corporation (Canada) Limited, which in turn had a subsidiary in tax-free Singapore. This "round robin" meant that $50 million of Canadian money went into a Canadian company. From the Canadian company it went into a Singapore company, where no tax was involved. In turn the money was used in the Singapore company to repay bank loans which had been raised in Singapore, and money eventually ended up in the New Zealand Shipping Corporation.
Let us go around the other way: the net effect of this was that the New Zealand-I was going to say "schemer", but let us call him a very talented lawyer, had worked out a deal whereby he was able to raise $50 million of Canadian money to finance New Zealand's ships in order to carry out trade not only with Canada but throughout the world. This was done on the basis that there was no tax paid on any revenue coming to Canadians with respect to the $50 million. Passing this money through Singapore meant that they could convert what left Canada in the form of capital funds to debt funds. Therefore, in Singapore it then became a loan going to New Zealand and was a deductible item by those who borrowed the money in
Customs Tariff
New Zealand. In short, the little wrinkle ended up being a 9 per cent or 10 per cent charge in New Zealand, deductible from income tax there, went through Singapore, came into Canada, was then paid out in the form of a dividend to Canadians who had bought those preferred shares, and, as Hon. Members know, there is no tax on dividends in Canada if they are paid from Canadian dividend-paying corporations.
This is the type of thing we should be looking into, the type of thing that the Government, until drawn to its attention, was totally unaware of. In fact, the Government, through Revenue Canada, had given what is called a "comfort letter"; a ruling in more positive terms, stating that the wrinkle was fine, go ahead and pickup the $50 million in Canada, finance your shipping fleet, they do not have to pay any taxes in Canada, and if they want to make it a deductible item as far as the interest is concerned down in New Zealand, more power to them. That, in effect, was the National Revenue ruling on that little wrinkle. When this matter was brought to the attention of the Minister, he, of course, professed to be quite annoyed, and I understand there was quite a bit of commotion between Finance and Revenue over the whole affair.
I raise this, Mr. Speaker, because here we go again. The Government, rightly or wrongly, has entered into an arrangement or an agreement with New Zealand, and rather than coming openly to this Parliament and saying this is what they have done, they need our approval and this is why they feel we should give our approval, and have it all open and above board, we find it is up to its old tricks, trying to sneak it in. It is put into a Bill in the hope that no one would be alerted and realize what the Government has in mind.
I suggest it is time for this House to be alert, to ask the Government, as I hope to myself, some pertinent questions concerning this agreement touching on trade between New Zealand and ourselves. Above all, I urge other Members of this House to do likewise, because surely the time has come that this Government, and especially the emperor, who is away on another trip, I understand, should not be allowed to take the House of Commons for granted any longer.
On two points I urge all Members to at least consider this legislation and possibly speak on the Bill. If they are concerned about metrication in this country and its consequences, speak to clause 5 in Bill C-90. If they are concerned about these rather secret arrangements which are tucked into legislation to get parliamentary approval, then speak on the Bill generally because they will find many references to the New Zealand trade agreement in this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the matters raised by the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) are a concern. The continued acceleration, if you will, in the imposition of the metric system is a concern. I think a lot of people in the country are expressing some concern about the difficulties confronting them as they try to deal day by day with the changeover. I think this goes back to its inception, and

November 9, 1982
Customs Tariff
I am sure every Member of the House, with the benefit of hindsight, now realizes that there are problems.
At the time metrication was brought in, it was with the general support of Members of this House, including the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling), whose comment at the time of the debate was that they should accelerate the bringing forth of the metric system. It was not being done quickly enough. That is not intended to be a criticism of the Hon. Member; I say it only because I think it shows that we all learn with the passage of time and from the experiences which affect the people in the country.
I think, Mr. Speaker, the Government learned, along with the rest of us, that there are people who are genuinely concerned about this continued imposition. That the changeover is difficult, there is no question. For the adult population the changeover from our existing weights and measures to the metric system has been a particularly difficult changeover. It has been costly, for small businesses in particular but for all business in general. It has not generated the industrial growth in Canada which one might have hoped for in providing the alternative measuring devices, whether they be weigh scales or other equipment which is necessary for the changeover. There has been very little in the way of a Canadian industry emerging as a result of this change. Must of the money being spent in the changeover is being spent outside of Canada.
I think that, as with many things, this House of Commons could well take a look at where we go from here. In fact, as I look at this from what I hope is a practical point of view, the changeover has in many ways reached a point where it would be more costly perhaps to go back than it would be to leave it in place. I do not think anyone is suggesting that we should make an attempt to revert back. I think the cost of doing that would probably be as great as or greater than the cost of leaving things as they are. I say this from a practical and nonpolitical viewpoint. However, I do think that the changes which are continually being introduced are made without careful enough consideration and the Hon. Member for York-Peel raises that as a legitimate point. I think the Government ought to consider that.
However, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with the general thrust of the legislation for a few moments. I think I speak for most if not all of my colleagues in this party, and I suspect for a number of my colleagues outside of my party, when I say that the continued move towards a tariff-free world is, in the hypothetical or academic sense, a laudible goal. If it ever happens, it will probably in the end prove to be beneficial. But at the moment my worry about it is that we are inching towards it little by little without giving careful thought to the implications of the changes. It is all well and good for us to negotiate with others to reduce tariffs in the hope that we will open up new markets and assist other countries in their development. However, my experience has been that we have not benefited a great deal from the already negotiated reduction in tariffs. My experience has been that even in those countries where we were able to arrive at an understanding with regard to a reduction in general tariffs, there are other
barriers which are either being put in place or were already in place prior to the reductions coming into effect.
As an example of that, Mr. Speaker, I think those who have been to Japan or worked with the Japanese would appreciate that, although we might enter into any number of agreements with that country as to a reduction in tariffs, it is very difficult to imagine how this would benefit us. It might, in a global sense, appear to be a move toward something which will ultimately be worthwhile. But in the immediate sense of the effect it has on Canada and Canadian industry, it is extremely difficult to put any kind of accurate measurement on any benefit which flows to Canadian industry as the result of a reduction in tariffs between this country and Japan. If anything, when we do reduce tariffs all we do is make it easier for them to sell in our country, but because of the nature of Japan, because of non-tariff barriers-not always governmental nontariff barriers but barriers nonetheless-we have not really opened up any markets for ourselves.
I noted with interest when I was visiting Japan that to a great extent, even if you were to have no tariffs of any kind, it would be very difficult for us to penetrate the Japanese market simply because the single largest barrier to the sale of Canadian-made products in Japan is the sense among the Japanese that they ought to buy products made in Japan, not products made outside of their country. Because of this very strong sense of loyalty to their own economy and development, indeed to their own products, even without any tariffs at all-we would find that we have not benefited one iota in terms of increasing our ability to manufacture and therefore to sell. On the other hand, because we in Canada do not have that same sense of loyalty, if you will, to Canadian manufactured products, we would be opening up our market to the Japanese.
I think we really have to have a discussion on that at some point in this House. We have to do this with an eye to understanding what it is we are hoping to achieve as a result of the tariff reduction negotiations which go on. I think we clearly have to understand the benefits, whatever they may be, and the possible problems that may develop from this continued reduction, little by little, in the tariff wall that was in place, presumably for the purpose of allowing our industry to grow.
For some reason that discussion does not take place in the House of Commons. I am not too sure that it will take place as a result of what I say today, but I hope my comments will generate in the minds of Hon. Members questions about why we have tariffs at all, why we have them in certains areas, what the over-all benefit or disadvantage would be as a result of the reduction of certain tariffs, how we propose to protect our growing industry base from massive intrusions from outside, and what we would use as an alternative to developing the industry base. Then we could make a decision about the level of tariffs and the variety of areas of commerce.
We are going to be faced with very serious problems in the not too distant future in this country. We are already facing
November 9, 1982

problems now, although they are minor compared to the problems we will ultimately face unless we restructure our economy.
It has proven to be of great advantage to this country that we were resource rich. Those resources have been the backbone of the development of this country and the means of providing the kind of substantial wealth that was so necessary to ensure the standard of living that most Canadians have enjoyed over the last few years. I do not think anyone denies that to continue to rely on that resource wealth alone would be very foolish. It would not enable us to provide for the next generation, and perhaps the one following that, the same opportunities that were provided for us by those in positions of power in the generation that preceded us.
I am concerned that we in this House should find a way to give some focus to what I think is a growing concern among Canadians. I believe that Canadians expect us to have some clear picture of where we would like Canada to be 25, 30 or 40 years from now, what kind of economy we will have then and what its base will be. If it is to be a manufacturing economy, which areas of manufacturing are we likely to excel in? Which areas are likely to grow and which areas are less likely to grow? Which areas are vital to the maintenance of the communities which lie so far apart in the country and are therefore not as interdependent as such communities are in many other countries? What would we do to protect the economic base of the many communities from coast to coast?
We must make these fundamental decisions before we enter another round of tariff reductions. It could well be that even in the 1980s and the 1990s it will be necessary for us to maintain some degree of tariff protection in certain areas of our industrial development in order that those areas will be able to grow, based on the domestic market capability of Canada and Canadians.
I sometimes suspect that the changes the Government makes are made in isolation from reality. The Government decides to make a reduction in certain areas because someone thinks that would be to their advantage, without considering whether that reduction might be very damaging to a fledgling industry. It might have the capacity to fill more of Canada's needs but suddenly finds itself made vulnerable by the reduction and in the period of early growth is not able to compete with larger industry from outside the country and then, to all intents and purposes, is rendered of little value and becomes redundant.
There are areas where the tariffs are being reduced as a result of this legislation or where they are non-existent. I think we should consider what this will do to industry. We should do an analysis of this in the House of Commons, and I hope the new rules will allow that kind of thing to occur through a committee, for example. In an industry where there is no tariff protection or where it is extremely small, perhaps before the legislation is passed we could do an analysis to determine what effect the changes would have.
I am not interested in whether the Government, through its advisers and experts, has done some analyses superficially or in
Customs Tariff
depth. I have no way of knowing that, but I am interested in knowing, as someone representing a manufacturing community, what impact tariff changes, reductions or eliminations will have on the industries located in the area that I represent or that some of my colleagues represent. I should like to know this in advance of the changes being put into effect.
For example, Mr. Speaker, the imposition of metric was not thought out clearly enough, and because of that we ran into difficulties. It was done with the best intentions in the world but it turned out to be not as useful as we had thought it would be. 1 suggest that that is true of many of the tariff changes recommended in this Bill.
What I am really saying is that I do not think we are told nearly enough about what is intended. I do not think the analysis is really complete enough. It would not be appropriate for us to continue along the lines we have been following in granting reductions year after year, in advance of making a decision about where our strength will lie. We should know the kind of manufacturing we anticipate for the next one or two decades and the kind of assistance that will be necessary to make sure that growth industries are given a fair shot before they are opened up to the tough world of competition against others who may be well established and capable of undercutting them in their formative years.
1 have a great deal of reluctance to deal with the legislation as it stands, Mr. Speaker. I would ask, for example, without knowing but by reading the Bill, why we should open up our borders, eliminate all tariffs and have no protection in areas such as 47605-1 of Schedule III which deals with items related to hospitals, operating and other devices necessary for the maintenance of an adequate health care delivery system. I would ask myself, in addition to other things, why we would eliminate the tariff there rather than look around to see whether or not there is in Canada an industry base capable of producing these items and then make a decision as to what assistance it requires in order to strengthen it in world terms. Also I would ask myself what we could do to develop that industry, if it is deemed to be of value, or whether it is necessarily good that there be no tariff at all during the period when the industry is being encouraged to develop. That could be said of a number of things. I will not go through them one by one but I may do so in Committee.
I have a feeling that we may be going about this backwards. We are going about the opening up of trade in a wrong-headed way. I feel that we are making the final decision before making the early ones, or that we have not made decisions in an orderly manner to enable us to come to proper conclusions. We have not made decisions about who is to be assisted and in what way before we decide to eliminate tariffs. Of course, we realize that once the tariffs are eliminated it is virtually impossible to put them back in place again. Once gone, they are generally gone forever. Therefore, to make the decision in isolation from the over-all economic decisions which must be

November 9, 1982
Customs Tariff
made about where the country is going does not make much sense.
In any event, 1 raise these matters because I have a feeling there will come a day in the House of Commons when, as the Hon. Member for York-Peel indicated, Liberal Members and others might have second, third and fourth thoughts about the matter, such as some have about metric. I have the feeling there will be people in the House of Commons who will have second, third and fourth thoughts about what we did with tariff protection, how we lost an industry base as a result of negotiating away protection and what it will cost in terms of subsidy of one kind or another to try to maintain the industry base if, as and when the protection of tariffs is no longer there.
I predict that there will be a raging debate some day in the House of Commons centred around how we protect the industries we are attempting to encourage to develop. One question raised will be whether we should put in place some kind of tariff. I am sure that question will be asked. Then those who will be making that decision will look at us and ask why we gave it away in the first place without giving enough thought to what would happen down the road.
I suppose my comments are really a caution. I hope that some time over the course of next year one or other of the Standing Committees of the House of Commons will be charged with the responsibility of taking a look at the impact of reductions and eliminations of tariff protection which have taken place over the course of the last decade. Hopefully it will look at the industries most affected, analyse the impact of the changes and try to decide or come up with some definitive answers about whether or not any benefits flowed to Canada and, if so, what they were and what they were worth both in terms of the development of the economy and in terms of the safeguarding of the industry base which appears to be fleeing every day.
Finally, in looking back over the years the only reason many of our industries located here was because their parent companies, whether in Great Britain, France or more recently in the United States, decided that in order to penetrate the Canadian market and to compete with existing Canadian companies they should locate some of their manufacturing capacity in Canada. We are not necessarily over the hump, so to speak, in terms of economic growth. I do not think we have reached the point of going it alone.
I cannot help looking back over the course of the last three years and thinking of what has happened to the automotive industry. We have the auto pact. It was an agreement between Canada and the United States intended to benefit Canada. It created a tariff-free zone in automotive trade. Presumably the end result when it was first established was to establish in Canada manufacturing, research and development capabilities which would enable industry to grow. That did not come to pass. I think most people would agree that the free trade arrangement has been manipulated over its lifetime. The parts manufacturing, which we all anticipated would come to Canada as a result of the arrangement, really did not come here. We ended up with many years of favourable balance in terms of dollar for dollar trade, but we did not end up with a
manufacturing capability because the favourable balance was generally on assembled vehicles rather than on the manufacture, and therefore on the development, of the parts.
Recently that hit us very hard. Many of us analysed it in an attempt to see what were the possible solutions. It became even more complicated with the growth of the Japanese industry, which was able to penetrate not only the Canadian but the North American market. It was able to work out arrangements between its manufacturers, as did some European manufacturers, and the manufacturers of so-called North American vehicles. The best example would be Renault and AMC, two of the companies which came together. This presumably allowed Renault to bring vehicles into the United States, and because it was part of AMC, to transfer them through the United States and into Canada without normal tariff restrictions. Whether it actually occurred in that way is questionable, but certainly it was in their minds.
I asked myself at the time whether that was what we intended or what benefit we would obtain from it. To put it crudely, it seems that all we got out of it was being shafted. I am not referring to making drive shafts; I am referring to another kind of shafting.
I wonder if that is where we are going, if that is what this is all about, and if that is where we will end up. If it is, we must stop it soon or we will be in serious trouble. That would be a good industry sector for the House of Commons to concentrate on for a while because it employs or at least employed substantial numbers of people in central Canada, particularly in Ontario and Quebec. Without making a case for the Province which I represent, there is grave concern about where the industry is going, what the impact of the auto pact will be, and whether or not they will be able to bring in engines from Japan and other parts of the world, through the United States, across the border and into Canada under the auto pact, even though the engines were not manufactured in those countries. There is serious question as to whether or not that will happen or indeed is happening.
One cannot have a discussion of the Customs Tariff and the repeal of or reductions in the Customs Tariff without taking a look at the implications. I use the automobile industry as an example, but it is not the only example of what can and does occur.
What are we going to do now to get benefit to Canada? How are we going to reclaim, if there is to be any reclaiming done, any benefit for ourselves? Who is going to gain any employment from it, other than those who sell and perhaps service vehicles? Are we going to try now to negotiate back, if you will, to a point where we will insist on a value added component of one kind or another, and what will it be? What will we use as the lever to get this benefit in the event we want to get it to pry loose some of the manufacturing that we ought to have in this country from its home base and bring it into Canada so that Canadians will get benefit?
November 9, 1982

Those are difficult questions. I am not pretending for a moment that they are necessarily answerable in one afternoon. Nor do I pretend that everyone in the House of Commons automatically will agree that that is a goal. I just put it forward as my opinion, and my opinion is as valid, I guess, as anybody else's. I raise the matter from that point of view.
It reminds me of an instance many years ago that caused a chuckle or two. When I was in the Ontario legislature I recall having difficulties over the importation of glazed cherries from France. People who manufacture glazed cherries in Canada were finding it extremely difficult to compete with the cherries imported from France even though there was tariff protection. We could not find out what was happening. After much investigation it was discovered that the French government was subsidizing sugar, which is the main component of glazed cherries. Because the French government was subsidizing sugar, it was, in effect, reducing the price which enabled manufacturers in France, to undercut those in Canada. I think this situation continues to happen in a number of interesting and devious ways.
I feel that legislation such as this should be the last step in the long process of analysing, developing and putting into place a strategy for Canadian development, manufacturing and other kinds of development. After you have done that and once you have it in place, you begin the process of making it easier for others to compete with us. But before that, we want to make sure that competition will be both fair and, to the extent that we can, of advantage and beneficial to Canada.
I suggest that it might be advisable, before we ever deal with another piece of legislation like this, that the House of Commons give careful thought to the comments and the intent of the comments I have made this afternoon. I do not expect the comments themselves to be bedtime reading for everybody, but I do think the intent is clear. I want to be sure that we are not making another mistake and digging ourselves more deeply into a hole than we dug ourselves into some time ago, a hole which we are having a great deal of difficulty getting out of.

received in return for reducing our tariffs on these products to New Zealand? What advantages will New Zealand give to us?
I would like to use this opportunity to elaborate on what I think is a fundamental error which is being made in this country. It concerns the notion that we can gradually lower our tariff barriers because other countries are supposedly doing the same thing without giving too much real consideration to the problems which have been created, which we are facing now and which will be created in the future by this very piecemeal process we are engaged in.
Canadians are living through a major recession. Indeed, Don McGillivray, the national economics editor for Southam, described our current situation as no longer a recession but a depression. I remind the Minister that there are now 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. Our manufacturing industries are not just suffering temporarily. Tens of thousands of workers in our Canadian industries have been laid off. Many of them have not just been laid off because of a temporary recession and things will get better next month, next year or the year after; they have been permanently laid off because the plants in which they worked for many years are now closed.
We accepted, I think much too easily, the myth that if all the industrialized countries were to reduce their tariffs, we would all benefit. I suppose Canada is the only country which took that idea seriously. We have been reducing our tariffs. While some other countries have reduced their tariffs, they have found a host of non-tariff ways to keep products of other countries out of their country.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain referred to Japan as an example. He suggested the reason foreign products are not sold in Japan to any great extent is that the Japanese people are loyal, patriotic and insist on buying Japanese products almost exclusively. That may be part of the reason but it is the smallest part. The real reason is that the Japanese have found a host of non-tariff ways to keep foreign goods out of their country. If a Canadian manufacturer or a manufacturer in some other country wants to sell in Japan, it can take up to three years of testing by the Japanese to see whether the product meets their standards.
A few years ago the electrical and electronic manufacturers met with Members of Parliament from this Party, and I am sure from other Parties. They discussed the possibility of the Japanese buying our generators. They said that Canadian manufacturers are efficient and competitive with other countries in the production of electrical generators. We were told that the Japanese electrical companies could not even look at a Canadian bid unless the electrical generator industry in Japan was at 100 per cent capacity. Only then could it look at a bid from Canada or some other country. Countries belonging to the European Common Market, by the use of various techniques, are keeping out goods or reducing the sale of manufactured goods and agricultural products-

speechtext: I guess he didn't hear you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member began by relating his question to the question asked by the previous questioner dealing specifically with the agreement between Canada and New Zealand. He said, and I will try to paraphrase him correctly, that we are offering some change to New Zealand, offering a preference, a lower price or something like that. He then asked: "What did you get in return?" The point I tried to make in answer to the first question was that in that area of the Bill before us, under Clause 1 there is no change. The purpose of the agreement is to bring the agreement and relationship between the two countries up to date, but we did not change the tariff amount or schedules.
We did address the point of the Hon. Member who just asked the question that we should be concerned in all our relationships with our trading partners that they be efficient and beneficial to both Canada and New Zealand. The new agreement that is referred to in Clause 1 addresses the issues

specifically on these points. The agreement maintains the tariff treatment. Moreover, it establishes provisions for consultation and compensation. Mr. Speaker, I have the honour, on behalf of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), to move second reading of Bill C-129, an Act to amend the Bretton Woods Agreements Act and the International Development Association Act, referred to as the IDA Act.
The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, or the World Bank, was established near the end of the Second World War, first to assist in the rebuilding of war-torn Europe, and then subsequently to help in fostering economic development in developing countries.
In 1960, in order to accelerate the work of the World Bank in the very poorest countries of the world, member countries of the World Bank established the International Development Association, or IDA. Canada was a founding member of both
November 9, 1982

institutions to which I have referred, and through the years support of the World Bank and IDA has remained and will remain an important and secure part of Canada's aid program.
In 1980, the Government of Canada committed itself to reversing the trend of the last years of the 1970s and to expanding Canada's Official Development Assistance Program to 0.5 per cent of GNP by the middle of the decade and to use its best efforts to achieve 0.7 per cent of GNP by the end of the decade. In the economic statement of last week, the Minister of Finance reaffirmed this commitment. While planned ODA expenditures will be somewhat less than were planned a year ago, they will still be growing nonetheless at a strong pace and will absorb a growing portion of our national product. This growth will allow Canada to meet its international commitments both through bilateral and multilateral aid.
The World Bank and IDA are the single most important multilateral institutions in the world dedicated to fostering economic health and well-being. Working on the base of a small amount of cash provided by governments, recently just
7.5	per cent of the Bank's capital, the World Bank went out and used the remaining callable capital guaranteed by governments to borrow in the international capital market. These resources were then lent to developing countries on commercially related terms for economic development projects.
These projects are carefully chosen and evaluated by World Bank staff in co-operation with local authorities in user countries to ensure that the projects are well designed and have a high rate of return. For example, in 1982 the World Bank approved some 150 loans valued at over $10.3 billion to more than 43 developing countries.
On the other hand, IDA depends almost totally on government contributions to fund its program of long-term loans on very concessional terms to developing countries with annual per capita incomes below $730. However, IDA projects must also maintain the same high quality characteristics of World Bank-financed projects to which I have referred and, where necessary, technical assistance is provided to ensure that the objectives of the projects are achieved.
In 1982, IDA approved 97 loans to 42 borrowing countries valued at some $2.7 billion. However, the contribution of the World Bank and IDA to the improvement in the quality of life in poorer countries far outweighs the reference to dollar value which I have just indicated. These projects are leaders in the assistance of building essential social infrastructures of user countries.
In the difficult world economic and financial situation, the needs of developing countries or poorer countries are particularly acute. At a time when they are faced with growing demands for a better quality of life for their people, lower demand and prices for their exports and higher debt loads have resulted in a reduced capacity for their governments to meet the needs of their citizens.
The World Bank and IDA are playing an important role in helping to sustain development programs in developing countries. In providing valuable foreign exchange, the Bank and IDA also help to stabilize the international financial system
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
and to maintain demand in developing countries for the exports of industrialized countries. I should like to emphasize this by repeating it. I think the point is obvious, that in providing valuable exchange the Bank and IDA also help to stabilize the international financial system and to maintain demand in developing countries for the exports of industrialized countries which contribute to the funds.
A lessening of aid at this time would further weaken the prospects for economic development in these countries both now and in the future. The related Bill C-130, being introduced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), to provide funding for a number of regional development banks of which Canada is a member will also assist in maintaining essential aid flows. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) referred to that Bill and indicated that it will be before the House shortly.
Bill C-129 will permit Canada to continue to help the World Bank and IDA carry out their present function in this important work. The first part of the Bill amends the Bretton Woods Agreements Act which governs Canada's participation in the World Bank. The amendment raises the value of the shares of the World Bank that can be purchased by Canada from the $1,112,200,000 currently in the Act to a new amount of $2,178,200,000. These obligations are measured in 1944 U.S. dollars which are currently equal to about $1.47 Canadian. In layman's language, the amendment will permit Canada to subscribe to some 10,410 World Bank shares valued at approximately $1,600 million in current Canadian dollars. This is equal to 3.19 per cent of the U.S. $40 billion general capital increase. However, only 7.5 per cent of the face value of the shares, or some $120 million Canadian, must actually be paid in over a four to five-year period. As I indicated, the remainder of our subscription is callable and represents a contingent liability for the Canadian Government.
Subclause 4(a) of the Bill amends the IDA Act in order to permit Canada to honour its commitments to the sixth in a series of resource replenishments of IDA since its founding in 1960. This sixth replenishment of IDA was negotiated in 1979 as a three-year $12 billion replenishment for the period 198183. Canada agreed to contribute 4.3 per cent, or $601.8 million Canadian.
Subclause 4(b) amends the Act to provide a supplemental contribution to IDA in order to provide some $200.6 million Canadian for IDA. This is a bridging year between its current or sixth replenishment and its next replenishment which will proceed in due course.
The bridging arrangement is required because what had been intended to be a three-year replenishment of IDA has extended into the fourth year due to delays in U.S.A. contributions. In order to avoid a drastic decline in IDA resources during the fourth year, other major donor countries, expect the U.S.A. and including Canada, agreed in Toronto during the World Bank's last annual meeting to make additional contributions to IDA of some $2 billion. I am sure it is apparent that

November 9, 1982
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
the Canadian delegation played a very prominent role in achieving this agreement.
The payments to the World Bank and IDA will be made in the form of non-interest bearing notes issued by the Minister of Finance over the next four years. Actual encashments of the notes will take place, however, over a number of years as the World Bank and IDA make disbursements on projects and programs in the developing countries. The budgetary implications of these amendments in any one year are, therefore, not large and have been taken into account in the budgetary forecasts of the Government.
In conclusion, I have some comments as to the importance and significance of the issues raised in the Bill before the House. I have made reference, of course, to large amounts of money and a number of figures.
As all Hon. Members probably know, developing nations have been hard hit by the one-two punches of higher oil prices followed by the international recession and high interest rates to which I have referred. Their finances and their borrowing capabilities are at present sorely strained.
In addition, the developed nations have been equally hit by the international recession, and in many cases have found themselves under pressure to curb assistance to the World Bank. Many of these uncertainties arose at the 1982 annual meetings of the Board of Governors of the International Bank held this September in Toronto. There was frankly, Mr. Speaker, deep concern that strains created by the delay in the U.S. contribution to the IDA could cause the crumbling of the current system of multilateral burden sharing. Notwithstanding that bridging agreement, the challenge to the supporter countries, to the Bank and to IDA remain and continue to exist. There will be challenges to all contributor countries.
This Bill before us today represents a confirmation that Canada will not desert the developing nations when they need help the most. This Bill is a confirmation not only to Third World nations themselves, but to developed nations, who under pressure at home-like Canada-might be considering cutbacks in support to Third World lending programs.
It is in that context that I call upon and urge all Members of the House to join the Government in making apparent the extent of support of Canadians in the commitment to these programs and to speed the support and consideration of this Bill, which is so badly needed by developing countries.
