speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are considering Bill C-129, to amend the Bretton Woods Agreements Act and the International Development Association Act. I am pleased to put before the House the position of the Progressive Conservative Party on this legislation. In doing so, I want to recognize the importance which these two very vital institutions have played over the past number of years, particularly in recent years, in the international financial markets of the country. They have maintained the stability of these markets by fostering economic growth in
some of the underdeveloped countries of the world. Through the complementary role they have played with the International Monetary Fund, they have helped countries to adjust and find ways out of their economic problems.
The purpose of the legislation is to increase funding available both to the World Bank-the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development-and to the International Development Association which will allow them to continue to play the very important role they have played over the years.
The first basic part of this legislation is to authorize an increase in the Canadian contribution to the World Bank as part of an over-all doubling of its capitalization. This will assist the World Bank to continue the lending programs it has undertaken over the years in its practice of lending development funds basically on a commercial basis.
The second part of the legislation is to provide funding to the International Development Association, which is the agency that provides loans on soft terms to the less developed countries of the world-the poorest countries-in order to help them develop and grow. These two agencies have played a vital role and have been critically important in the past 20 or 30 years to the workings of the world economy.
In considering this legislation, we should stand back and look at the position in the international economy today. I have to say that this position is not encouraging. There is inflation as a result of oil price shocks, basically negative growth in so many countries in the world today, high unemployment and balance of payments problems, all of which have eroded the stability of the international economy. There has been an increase in protectionism as pressures on many countries develop. This threat of increased protectionism causes even greater pressure on the system than has been the case.
Another problem has been the deflationary pressures on some of the major commodity prices. The extreme pressure which this puts on those less developed countries in the world who rely to such a great extent on the export of natural resources obviously has created problems for those countries.
Finally, the current slowdown in the industrialized countries of the world, the United States, Europe, Japan and Canada, in itself adds to the pressures that are being placed on the less developed countries of the world. The outlook for the immediate future obviously is very grim. It is important for the industrialized countries of the world to understand the impact of this grim outlook on their own economies. More than one-third of the exports of the United States, Japan and the European Community are to the less developed countries of the world. The situation for Canada is not quite the same, but exports are still a significant part of our economy. They are a growing portion and Third World countries are potentially a good source for our markets in the years ahead.
Canada can look at this request for increased funding in two ways. We are a developed country and we are an industrialized country. I think we have an important role to play in the growth of the international economy by getting our own house
November 9, 1982

in order, by getting our own inflation under control, by maintaining the monetary discipline that will lead to lower rates of inflation, and by controlling our deficits and government spending. Government spending has played such an important factor in the growth of inflationary pressures.
We must also look at the role we have played in improving our own productivity. We were reminded only two weeks ago of the fact that Canada's productivity record is the worst of the industrialized nations of the world. That is hurting our competitive position and causing more weakness in the over-all world economy because Canada is not pulling its weight. Canada is not doing the job it can do. People in this country have been urging the Government to perform. We can also consider the problems faced by the less developed countries in the world with a certain degree of empathy because, like them, we have a very extensive resource base which is a very important element in our balance of payments and economic position as a result of the jobs they create, the economic activity emanating from the mines, forests and so on in our country today.
We have suffered from the weakness in the metals markets. We see that only too clearly with the announcements out of Schefferville or Sudbury and in the Yukon and British Columbia. We also see the tremendous weakness in the forest products industry in British Columbia and in Ontario and the impact of energy prices on our energy industry today. These are all areas where we have suffered in the past year because of weakness in the over-all world economy, and those pressures which are felt in our country in those industries are very similar to the pressures felt in the less developed countries in the world. They have led to increased unemployment, particularly in those communities which are very reliant on the resource industries. There we have a very clear illustration of what is going on in some of the less developed countries which are totally reliant, for their export market, on the export of natural resources. Fortunately we have a stronger economic base. We have a manufacturing base and we export manufactured goods so that the impact of the world slowdown and deflationary pressures on mineral prices is, relatively speaking, less important to Canada as a whole but, obviously, is very important to those parts of the country which are directly affected.
I think we understand the position in which the less developed, poorer countries in the world find themselves today. However, we must also stand back and ask whether we are doing our part as important members of the world economic community, whether we are doing enough to bring back economic growth, or whether we could do better in addressing the needs of the world economy in the adjustment out of the very slow growth period we are in now, and in moving into an area of growth. We in the Conservative Party say that we must do better if we are to pull our weight in the world today. We must do better in productivity. We have not made any progress in productivity over the last three years. We have seen some progress in dealing with inflation over recent months, but it is
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
a very slow recovery and it is much more related to the tremendous weakness in the economy today than to any actions taken by the Government to reduce these inflationary pressures.
Job creating investment activity in the country today is very weak. It is one of the key elements in the slowdown of our economy. Control of deficits is the key element and has caused great concern to members in the world financial community. Our record in controlling deficits has been absolutely atrocious. I do not need remind Hon. Members that estimates of our deficit going from $10 billion to $20 billion, and now approaching $25 billion, give no sense of confidence that we have our own economic affairs under control. Finally, in economic growth, we are still very much at the bottom end of the list of industrialized countries. So, we are not doing our job. We are not doing as well as we could to help the world itself get out of the economic morass it is in today.
Because of bad decisions and inaction on the part of past Liberal governments, the effort of pulling ourselves out of the recession has been particularly painful. The recession is causing tremendous problems in unemployment as well as tremendous social and political problems. The transition to recovery has been very slow and leaves us just that much more exposed to continuing economic problems in the international economy. However, as our recovery continues to be slow, we are unable to help in world economic recovery as we could if we were a healthier country. We must remind ourselves today of the fact that we are a part of the international economic community, and the more we can do to help ourselves, the more we could do to help other countries in the world.
Developed countries are the key to the health of the world economy. If there is continued stagnation in the United States, Europe, Japan and in other countries, there will be greater and greater economic problems for the less developed countries. The most vivid example concerns the problems being experienced by Mexico, but we should not simply look at Mexico, because other countries, like Argentina, Brazil, Zaire and some of the other African nations, are undergoing excruciating domestic pressures.
The debate today is a reminder that although the Government continues to blame the world economy, we are part of that world economy and must do our utmost to help it by working to bring about a healthier and stronger Canadian economy. The November budget had a very negative impact on job creating investment. The National Energy Program did tremendous damage to the oil and gas industry in the country, the one industry which was performing very well. The performance of the Foreign Investment Review Agency has slowed down economic activity in the country, as a result of obstacles it placed in front of that process. All these were wrong policies, policies which inhibited economic recovery in Canada.
I think we need only remind ourselves of the report in the paper this morning wich illustrated that the performance of the Foreign Investment Review Agency in the past few months

November 9, 1982
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
has been turned around quite considerably from its performance in the previous two years. You must ask yourself, Mr. Speaker, why did the Government take over two years to implement these changes in the Foreign Investment Review Agency process? They are fundamentally the same changes to which we had agreed in 1979, in a Conservative Cabinet, which asked the Provinces for their comment before implementation. Once the comments came back from the Provinces, nothing was done by the present Government for two years. Therefore, we suffered during that two-year period, and the statistics in the paper demonstrate how easy it was for the Government to change that direction. However, the blockheaded nature of the former minister of industry, trade and commerce in following his own extreme nationalist thinking in stopping investment in the country has caused some of the problems we are facing today and has certainly exacerbated our unemployment problem.
Therefore, we should play our role in getting our own house in order so that we can alleviate the strains of people here in Canada, the pressures about which we read in the newspapers and in letters from our constituents, concerning the break-up of families, the increase in the divorce rate, suicides, increased crime rate and increased alcoholism. These are the social pressures that we see in Canada. However, when one considers the much more severe social and economic problems in the less developed countries in the world, we see the impact on our country in a microcosm.
The economic stresses also lead, in a very real way, to the protectionist pressures to which I referred a minute ago. We see this directly in the United States because there is such a direct impact upon our own country as a result of the number of bills before Congress today, the action taken by Congress in the trucking industry, the threat to our forest products industry and the "Buy American" legislation. These affect us directly. However, because some of those bills have a very broad effect in the world today, they will also affect the rest of the world, particularly the less developed countries which do not have the strength in their economies to resist the pressures such as Canada is able to do.
At the same time that we see these problems developing, we should consider the aggregate balance of payments deficit in the less developed countries which will have approached $90 billion in this current year. In aggregate, it will amount to some $500 billion. We look at the twin problems against that background of the high interest rates-and let us not forget that 10 per cent and 15 per cent interest rates today are still extremely high considering the huge $500 billion debt of those less developed countries-and the current practices of the commercial banks. They are pulling back somewhat from the role they have played because of the extent of the risk that they are exposed to, the extensive nature of the problems in the less developed countries, as well as the potential losses they are facing, particularly in view of the very real problem of the Mexican situation today.
This is the background to the legislation before us today on which we consider the request by the World Bank and IDA to replenish their capacity to lend money to the rest of the world today and particularly to those Third World countries.
I would remind the House that the World Bank lends money to the faster developing countries on harder terms, comparable to commercial terms, while the IDA is lending money on soft terms which are basically grants. Their terms are 50 years with no interest.
Let us review some specific numbers in relation to what is happening in the commercial banking community today. These figures illustrate a problem being faced by the poorer nations and the consequent relative increase in the importance of the World Bank and the International Development Association. Despite an increase of $16 billion in the aggregate current account deficit of the non-oil developing countries last year, bank lending to those countries increased only marginally, from about $49 billion in 1980 to $50 billion in 1981. The financing by this bank lending rose from approximately 39 per cent during the 1974-75 period to almost 60 per cent in 1979 to 1980. In 1981, the borrowing from banks fell back to approximately 50 per cent of the financial requirement. Obviously, there is a greater role for these international lending agencies to play.
Commercial bank lending to the low income countries and other net oil importers has obviously declined. Bank lending to the low income countries also fell during this same period, from a peak of almost $3 billion in 1979 to less than a billion dollars in 1981. This occurred during a period when the aggregate deficit of these countries rose by almost 40 per cent. The most marked deceleration in bank lending has been experienced by a group of the less developed countries known as the net oil importers. That is the background that we are looking at today. It clearly points out the important role that must be played by the multilateral lending agencies.
Clearly, the role of the commercial banks has declined due to the fragile nature of today's financial system, and the importance of the World Bank and IDA has increased, particularly in the case of the International Development Association. I am not suggesting that the role of the great international banks as key interveners will substantially be transferred to these international agencies, but there is a bigger job to be done and there is clearly an important need for the multilateral lending agencies today.
Canada must take its role seriously in fostering the stability of the international financial system. In a time of international financial stress, multilateral co-operation is a key factor in economic development, as is aiding the International Monetary Fund, the IMF, in its role of helping those countries through the adjustment process needed because of that economic stress I have mentioned.
As I have said, we must get our own economic house in order in particular to participate in the economic recovery that we so clearly need today. However, we also have a responsibility to our partners. Canada is one of the seven members of the Summit nations. Being a member of the Organization for
November 9, 1982

Economic Co-operation and Development, we are also one of the leading industrial countries in the world. We are not making use of our country's untold natural benefits which include natural resources, mineral resources and energy resources. We are not making use of our ability to produce such vast quantities of food to the extent that we should.
Two weeks ago I reminded the House of the position of Canada in the world today. Of 81 countries in the world, measured by Euromoney in a composite measurement of economic growth, control of inflation, the competitive position of the country and its performance on the exchange rate, we are number 40. This is evidence that we are not doing nearly as well as we should be doing. For this reason we must get our economic house in order. Not enough is being done to assist this recovery and to reduce the volatility and instability in the international financial community. We must do more to restore confidence in our economy. Through that, we can do our part in aiding the rest of the world.
Against that background, let us consider Bill C-129 which is a Bill to increase financing, for the World Bank and the International Developing Association. We must ensure adequate funding for these agencies because of the magnitude of the international problem. I am not suggesting for a minute that problems can be solved by simply handing out money. We must also recognize that there is a limited amount of capital in a country such as Canada and the other industrialized countries of the world.
We must recognize, however, that aid is only part of the solution. The key to recovery of the less developed countries is to fight protectionism and keep the world trading system open. This is far more important than aid. Canada must do everything it can to resist protectionist pressures both within our borders and that of the other countries which are so important to us such as the United States, Japan and the European countries. We must fight protectionism in order to allow the less developed countries in the world continued access to world trading markets. If they do not have that access to the markets or to the technology transfer that can take place in the developed countries of the world, the world community will face serious problems in ten or 15 years.
That, too, is only a small part of the problem. Today we are focusing on the purpose of this Bill which is to provide more money for the over-all development process. Money is a very important element in the supportive role which developed countries can play in the recovery of the less developed countries of the world. Under the provisions of this Bill, the International Development Association is requesting approximately $600 million. We should understand that this will be drawn down over a ten year period. It is called the Sixth Replenishment. As the Minister pointed out, it is expected that that replenishment will look after the needs of the IDA for approximately the next three to four years.
Canadians must participate in this program because the International Development Association is the most important
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
agency in the world today to assist the less developed countries. Confidence in the international financial system depends on the willingness of developed countries to play a role through multilateral agencies like the World Bank and the International Development Association.
If Canada and other countries do not play that role, the commercial banks will start to withdraw as well. If they see the confidence of governments of developing countries slipping in their ability to survive in the present state of the world, they too will slip. There is more need today for co-operative work between the commercial banking sector and the multilateral international financial agencies. The lack of such co-operation will result in a severe recession, and a depression will possibly follow.
Canada has an option. The Minister did not refer to it directly in his comments. Under the International Development Association rules, there is an agreement whereby if the United States does not take its full share of the requirements of IDA, other countries do not have to pick up their share. They can cut back on a pro rata basis comparable to the United States.
The United States has cut back significantly. It has cut back its participation at this time to less than 50 per cent of that which it would have to do if it were to play its full role. Other countries, including Canada, could also cut back. Others have not. I do not believe that Canada should cut back.
We believe Canada should continue to play the role it has played in the international financing community because of the importance of this lending and the effect which withdrawal of this lending could have if the tendency initiated by the United States spread to other countries. The overwhelming consensus at the World Bank meetings in Toronto in September was that the amount the IDA is asking for is an appropriate amount. The United States did not agree. It said that the extra money would make the fund act too quickly to save countries from the consequences of their own improvidence. There is a belt tightening that is going on and is necessary in the world today.
The United States is uncomfortably aware that doubling the national contributions can have a very important impact on their internal financial problems, because the United States is a 20 per cent participant. That is an extremely large role for the United States to play relative to its size in the world community. That would amount to a $13 billion contribution, a very large amount of money.
Even though the United States has cut back almost all its contributions, if not all, countries have decided to pick up their pro rata share and have supported the International Development Association in this way. Having said that, I believe the Government of Canada should assess its position very carefully on an ongoing basis. Can we continue to play as large a role as we have in supporting these multilateral institutions? If our economic performance continues the same, if we continue to have a weak economy, particularly when we come out of the recession on a world-wide basis, we in Canada may have to cut

November 9, 1982
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
back. This places a greater emphasis on doing what we can in Canada to get our house in order.
1 also mentioned the problem of procurement for the World Bank and IDA for the goods and services needed to complete the projects. Canadian companies are not getting their pro rata share. This has been a matter of continuing concern to those in the Conservative Party.
Over the years we have seen an increased role the Canadian companies have been able to play, going from about 1.3 per cent about ten years ago to the current level of about 2.7 per cent. That amounted to about $730 million in 1981, but it was not enough. It does not give us our pro rata share which is something just short of 4 per cent. Therefore we have further to go on the question of procurement and the importance of providing jobs in this country, not in the United States, Germany or Japan which are competing with us to supply these projects.
Finally, the Government must consider whether our aid and development money is being spent as carefully, with as little waste as possible and in the best interests of the receiving countries. There is on ongoing debate in Canada on this subject. As we are in a recession, spending of this magnitude is a very important consideration on the part of Canadians in seeing how the Government spends the taxpayers' money. Can we afford this kind of money?
When the Conservative Party was in Government in 1979, we authorized a full review of the role that multilateral agencies play in our aid programs, as well as the role which CIDA plays. This review was to commence in the early part of 1980. It has not yet taken place. We in the Conservative Party feel this review must take place so that people in this country who are concerned over the role and the performance of our aid program will have the opportunity to state their case and have it aired in a public forum so that there can be a full, hard-nosed debate on the merits of our aid program and what Canada should be doing. We want to have that open debate. I urge the Government to have this debate. It will be held shortly after the Conservative Party forms the next government. However, I urge this Government to move ahead with it soon because of the interests Canadians are showing in all these areas such as the role of the multilateral agencies, the non-government organizations, CIDA, the program projection I referred to, waste, the impact on receiving countries and so on.

speechtext:
The Minister says we will have to wait a long time. We will not have to do that. Call the election today and we will have that review of aid programs started by the middle of next year. We in the Conservative Party are still committed to that review and it will be carried out as soon as the election is completed.
In conclusion, it is my view that the World Bank and the International Development Association have an important role to play in the international financial community. It should continue to receive the support of Canadians. Some feel that more support should be given, others that considerably less should be given. The consensus reached by Canada and other industrialized countries of the world is that the amount requested in this legislation is about the right amount. Some feel that Canada's record of foreign aid performance can be improved upon. We agree. That is why we asked for that committee. We feel that if we are to control waste and all these other things I mentioned, there should be that open debate by a committee in order that the performance of Canada's foreign aid program can be improved considerably.
We must also keep under constant review the over-all level of aid and the balance between the multilateral agencies and the bilateral aid we make directly available to countries of our choice. All of these are important considerations. Taking all these factors into account, I want to say that the official position of the Progressive Conservative Party is that we support this Bill.

The commercial banks do not have the understanding of, nor have they really provided any assistance to, the developing countries, in fact, they have undermined them through their almost totally irresponsible behaviour throughout the 1970s in the expenditure of their petro-dollars. If the Hon. Member who has just spoken had been on the External Affairs Subcommittee on Canada's relations with Latin America, and had visited and talked to the people with whom the members of the Subcommittee did, he would not be quite so flattering and complimentary about the role of the commercial private institutions and, above all, the private banks, as far as the developing countries of this world are concerned, and indeed, as far as some of the developed countries are concerned.
It was the former Minister of Finance of Colombia, who was the only Minister of Finance of a vast number of developing countries, who refused the attempts of the private banking sector to give easy loans in the 1970s. He said, they were on their knees before us to try to get us to take out very, very large loans. The Minister of Finance at that time said he felt that going into such indebtedness would be a mistake. He was unpopular at the time, of course, but he proved to be right. All the Governments in that part of the world which we talked to agreed that the enormous overextension into loans at the instigation of the private banking sector, had been a very great mistake.
When the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) says that his main reason for supporting institutions like the World Bank or IDA is that if we do not, then maybe the commercial banks will not be as concerned about the developing world, 1 can only say to him that is absolutely the worst reason to argue for the support of international financial institutions.
The Hon. Member talks about the problems of the seventies and eighties in the international economic order. He talks primarily about the fact the banks may not be making quite as big profits as they made all during the seventies. He just seems to assume that, and perhaps the Government does as well, because we cannot persuade the Government that we should have at least a declaratory statute informing us where the major outflows of this private capital go. The Hon. Member never mentions the kind of profits the banks took out of the developing world. That is where they got most of their profits in the seventies. He never mentions that. Maybe the Hon. Member and the Government also feel that the banks and the
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
multinationals as well, somehow are going to save the countries of the less developed part of the world. I say, thank heavens for the IDA, which is what we are discussing in the second part of this Bill, and indeed for the World Bank as well, which is the first part of the Bill and is pretty routine.
The most important part in relation to the IDA, which was touched on by the Minister and the previous speaker, but I think not fully enough, is that Canada and, indeed, all other members of the IDA are going to commit supplementary resources, to the IDA, Canada, in the amount of $200,600,000. This is being done for one simple reason, not that the United States has simply, as the Minister said, delayed its contribution, but that it has quite deliberately decided to spread its $3.2 billion commitment over four years instead of three. No word of criticism was heard about why the United States was doing this, but according to its own word it is doing this because the Reagan administration has been extremely suspicious of the countries receiving development assistance through the IDA, arguing that they are sloppy in managing their economies and that the reason for that is that they know they can fall back on aid. This is a sort of chastisement to the recipients. I wonder if the Reagan administration or the Minister, or the Tory speaker have ever looked at the results of that aid, particularly in the poorest countries. Eighty per cent of the loans from IDA go to countries with per capita annual incomes of less than $410. The economic returns on the loans average 18 per cent plus and that is just the quantifiable returns. Non-quantifiable returns, of course, would include the development of institutions within the country's policy reforms, and so on. Furthermore, several former IDA recipients are now IDA donors. Finally, IDA loans have never exceeded 2 per cent of total investment in recipient countries over-all. I think if we were a bit more open in our criticism of this cutback by the Reagan administration to IDA, if we did not allow them to get away with the crazy argument that the countries are sloppy in managing their economies, when economic returns have averaged 18 per cent plus, it would be more desirable than simply not saying anything.
IDA is absolutely fundamental. No commercial banks are going to get into IDA No other organizations except in the bilateral areas are going to get into something like IDA Even in bilateral assistance, it probably will become less rather than more in the future.
I was interested when the Minister talked about the commitment of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) not to go back on the 0.5 per cent of GNP for Canadian aid by the middle of the decade and 0.7 by the end of the decade. Of course, because of the drop in GNP there will have to be extremely substantial reductions in Canada's aid program over the next several years, reductions which were already begun by the Minister of Finance in his economic statement the other day. It is not, therefore, too hopeful a scene, as far as Canadian development assistance is concerned. All the more reason, therefore, to be grateful for our contribution to IDA The idea, somehow, that Canada can only provide assistance to the less

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we heard from the Minister as he introduced this Bill that the requirement for these funds totalling an additional $1,066 billion arose as a consequence of our obligation to acquire shares in accordance with the provisions of the Bretton Woods Agreement. It is significant Mr. Chairman, if we examine the terms of that agreement, and in particular the Second Schedule thereof, that, with respect to the issue of the acquisition of shares and additional shares that you will find under the provisions of the general operative Clauses relative to additional subscriptions there is no obligation imposed upon any member country to acquire additional stock in the Bank. We were also told that the quantum of acquisition in terms of dollar value really represented an obligation to take down 7.5 per cent in actual cash, with the balance of 92.5 per cent to be allocated and taken down contingently with the issuing of notes of the Government of Canada.
If we examine the Clause specifically we find that:
The Minister of Finance may provide for payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development in the manner and at the times provided for by the Agreement therefor set out in the Second Schedule, of a sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole an amount equivalent to the subscriptions required or permitted from Canada, that is to say, two billion, one hundred and seventy-eight million, two hundred thousand United States dollars-
It is this additional requirement for funds, Mr. Chairman, to which I draw the attention of the House. This requirement increases by a total of $1,066 billion the funds to which Canada had originally subscribed. While it is true that of the additional subscribed shares referred to by the Minister only
7.5	per cent need be paid for in cash, there is nevertheless an outstanding obligation to pay for the balance.
We have heard from all Members of this House who have spoken, that they favour the provisions of this anticipated piece of legislation. We have been told that despite the fact we have severe economic circumstances facing us today, our obligation to the Third World over-ride the considerations which we as Members of Parliament have for our constituents and our country. We are dealing, Mr. Chairman, not with an inconsequential amount of money, but with an amount in excess of $1 billion. It was not long ago in this House when the Minister of Finance came before us and claimed, among other things, that we had severe economic problems. He said on page 5 of his prepared text that the recession has been deeper and longer lasting in Canada than the Government anticipated when the June budget was presented. We are going through the most severe economic turmoil since the 1930s. Yet tonight in this House we are presented with a Bill which calls on the taxpayers of this severe economically depressed nation to cough up an additional $1,066 billion, and I hear not a word of complaint from anyone speaking with respect to this issue. If any additional evidence was needed to prove that Members in this House are either silent by obligation or have lost contact with reality, it is surely this Bill and the way in which it has been received.
November 9, 1982

We are not dealing with ordinary financial circumstances in Canada; we are dealing with circumstances which are dire, and which, according to the Minister of Finance, are as severe as any since the 1930s. Ele went on to indicate that the thrust of Government policy should include, among other things, as referred to on page 12 of the printed text of his speech, the reduction in official development assistance of some $245 million. He also referred to the reduction in defence spending of $230 million. No papers accompanied the text of the speech of the Minister of Finance to disclose where the funds have come from and where we will look for the additional funds necessary for the project outlined by the Minister for the creation of additional jobs in Canada. The paragraphs of his speech which referred to that matter appear on pages 11 and 12 of the text where he speaks of creating 60,000 new jobs over a period of 18 months and 13,000 additional jobs in the housing field. According to page 11, the total would appear to be 400,000 jobs.
Let us analyse the effect of the obligation upon the Government of Canada to lay out $1,066,000. The effect is that we will have subscribed for stock in an international financial institution which is referred to as the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development. That bank will allocate the expenditure of those funds. The Government will have no control over whether one dime of those funds is spent in Canada to acquire products or services that will be used in the developing world. It will have no control, Mr. Chairman.
This is a further illustration of the remoteness with which funds contributed by the taxpayers of Canada can be dealt with, not by this Parliament, not by the Government of Canada, but by a foreign controlled financial institution.
I submit that we have an absolute obligation to deal with this Bill as an intrusion into the control mechanism that should be in place whereby the Government and this House should direct funds that are available for the creation of jobs in this economic climate. This has not been done, however.
I submit to the House that this Bill, including the Clause to which reference has been made and others to which reference will be made in this Committee, creates an opportunity for a genuine analysis of our foreign-aid programs, including those administered by CIDA and those administered in this fashion by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
It also bothers me to hear that the 92.5 per cent of the obligations undertaken by the Minister of Finance in the event of the Bill being passed, will be disclosed in the accounts of this country as a conditional liability. That will amount to 92.5 per cent of an additional $1,066,000,000. Recognizing the practice of the Government in the past, an issue which has been dealt with in this House, I seriously doubt that there will be any amount on the national accounts with respect to this quantum of money, other than a contingent liability for $1. That process in itself deserves examination. Having regard to the comments made by the Minister, I am concerned that this method of issuing debentures, and of issuing demand notes for
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
part of the liability undertaken by the Government of Canada, is out of step with reality when we examine our national accounts.
What we must look for when we deal with this substantial sum, is not the 7.5 per cent thereon, but the entire amount of the obligation. Members who might otherwise have been concerned about such a gigantic expenditure. It is important to note that when Canada originally undertook its obligations with respect to Schedule Second payments, as of 1970 the aggregate amount of that obligation, if we examine Schedule A of the Second Schedule, was $325 million. It is my intention, Mr. Chairman, not only to speak against this Bill but, given an opportunity and the support of enough Members who will call for a recorded vote, to vote against this Bill.
I think it is time that the eloquence that accompanies the statement of the need, apparently, of other people in the world, is supported by action on the part of those who believe that the obligations of the individual Member to the Third World are paramount. I also believe that it is incumbent upon Members of this House who genuinely believe that their responsibility, in these times particularly, is to their constituents, to see that they have an opportunity to express those views clearly by putting their constituents and Canada first.
I hope that before this matter is concluded enough Members of the House will be sufficiently concerned about the nation and about our economic plight to ask that the matter be put to a vote. If it is, let Members stand and disclose the position they would take with respect to an issue which calls upon Parliament to expend an additional $1,066,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, I have one or two comments and also some questions. I understood the Hon. Minister to say that $30 million will be paid now but that the total amount will be $2,178 million. If that is not correct, would the Minister so indicate when he is dealing with my comments?
We are talking about a lot of money. There is a growing feeling across the country that the priorities of the Government are open to question. At the present time we have many people in need. We have more than one million people unemployed. Many of those people have now exhausted their unemployment insurance and are either living on welfare or with the assistance of relatives. If they are living on welfare, it is a burden that has now been shifted on to the Provinces' shoulders with the federal Government paying some part.
Also in this country many of our native people are living in utter poverty. Sometimes 27 people are living in a house that should hold five. This is not a pipe dream, this is the truth. We have Indian children and Indian women who are not getting enough to eat. We have many white people having a difficult time making ends meet. They are existing on welfare or some other type of meagre pension.
It is time for the Canadian Government to start checking its priorities. I do not think anyone in Canada objects to helping those in need in other countries, but, Mr. Chairman, charity begins at home. If we close our eyes to the poverty and the misery of people living in this country, that is pretty sad indeed. If we cannot find sufficient money to help the Indian people, the white people, those unemployed, those without enough to eat-and let us not think that everyone in Canada does have enough to eat-then we should be thinking twice about sending $30 million somewhere else.
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
If I understood the comments so far, we are doubling our commitment in this program. Instead, we should be doubling our commitment to the people who provide this money before we start doubling an amount and sending it to places where we do not know what will be done with it. That bothers me and I am sure it bothers others in Canada. There is no indication who is going to get this money and where it is going to go. There are no checks and balances on this money and $2 billion is a lot of money. Surely if we are going to start giving away such a sizeable amount of money, we should have an agreement that provides checks and balances so that we know where that money is going and who is going to get it.
People from some Third World countries have told me that they would not give a dime to help Third World countries because the wrong people get it. Many of the people living in poverty do not get help. How much of this money is going to those who are doing the work or heading up the organizations? Maybe everyone is completely honest and sincere, I hope they are, but the Canadian people should be given details when we are providing this much money in aid.
Unlike the Hon. Member from the NDP who just spoke, I have a lot of faith in the banks. I find the banks to be pretty honest and above board. Sometimes I object to some of the things they do, but by and large the banks provide a service to the people of this nation. However, I would like to know what is being charged by the banks that give this service. What is the interest rate being charged? How does it compare with the banks in our own country, and what are they doing? In other words, it is not simply okay to say that we are going to give $30 million this year to this organization when hardly 1 per cent of the Canadian people knows where it is going, what it is for and what the checks and balances are on that amount. Again, how much overlapping is there?
The majority of churches in this country ask their congregations for contributions for other countries. Congregations provide a lot of money for this purpose. Some provincial governments match dollar for dollar. I know a gentleman in Calgary, an ex-minister of a church, who spends his entire time securing funds for which he can get matching amounts for medical supplies to help doctors and nurses in other countries aid the sick.
I want to say that helping other people is part of the Canadian way. Canadians want to have some assurance that this money is going where it will do the most good. If we have people hungry in our own country, then let us look after them. If there is not always enough to go around, then the logical thing to do would be to cut down the amount going outside the country. Again, are these amounts simply welfare payments to other countries? The Government should have an answer to this question. If they are, the Government is simply helping people to become parasites, waiting for someone else to look after them.
Some of these countries have resources which they are not developing. One country was high up on the agriculture list at

Bretton Woods Agreements Act
one time but received so many contributions that it is now way down the list and is depending on other countries more and more. The Government should be checking this type of situation. I object to following the thought that we will somehow help these people through their governments irrespective of their government's belief. I am not anxious to build up a communist state anywhere; I do not think it is any good for the people. However, when a country with a communist government gets this support and has control of it, and in some case it does, that government says: "This is our gift to you; keep us in office". It is not fair at all. We are building up a regime which might some day use its power to kill Canadians. Most Canadians do not want a communist state.
I want to raise another point. I was amazed when I heard a suggestion that the United Nations should be given the authority to tax Canadians. That would be a type of world government. If we ever get to that point, the smaller countries of the world would be submerged by international police forces. They would either have to pay or else. That is not the type of world I want.
I was a delegate to the European Parliament this last summer and I was amazed to hear one of the elected members start to talk about their parliament having authority to levy taxes on the 11 countries which belonged to that organization for defence purposes. They do not have that authority yet, but if they ever do, pity the poor countries like The Netherlands and Belgium which could be forced to do almost anything that the majority wanted, without any sovereignty. Sovereignty would go out the window. Our Government should be carefully watching to see that we are not playing into the hands of a world government, because I am satisfied that 95 per cent of the people of Canada are opposed to that type of philosophy.
I want to finish my remarks by saying that I am not satisfied with the information the Government has given. I do not know where this money is going or who is getting it. I think there is a responsibility on the part of the Government to give that information to the people. I could go to the Salvation Army and say, "You have spent so much money, where did it go?", and the Salvation Army could give me a dollar by dollar account of it. They could tell me which of the world's countries it went into, what is being done with it and how their organization is helping people to help themselves. I could go to some of the Catholic organizations and they would give me the same information. Why can this Government not do the same thing? Why does the Government not ensure that it get the information and then give it to the people? Then we would find a swelling interest in helping more, particularly in helping people to help themselves. In the future we should help other people in the developing countries and other countries to help themselves. The main point today is that we should help people in Canada who are hungry, our native people and other Canadians who are not getting enough to eat. Let us make sure that we look after them first, because charity begins at home.

speechtext:
I am glad that the Minister has reverted to one of the questions which I had asked him earlier concerning our legal position with respect to liabilities upon our withdrawal. The Minister has just conjured up an image of our being paid for shares we have surrendered. I draw his attention to Article VI of the Agreement giving rise to our participation in this type of project which, in effect, deals directly with the issue of our subscription for shares in the Bank for Reconstruction and

November 9, 1982
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
Development. I would draw his attention, in particular, to Section 4(a) which provides:
When a Government ceases to be a member, it shall remain liable for its direct obligations to the Bank and for its contingent liabilities to the Bank so long as any part of the loans or guarantees contracted before it ceased to be a member are outstanding;-
The liability will remain for so long as any of those loans to which I made reference, made by the Bank on condition that those loans be guaranteed, with some of the deferred liabilities which we have pledged to the Bank, have been used for the purpose of raising money from commercial banks. That is, in fact, the conclusion to which one would come. It is the same conclusion one would come to with respect to the very simple illustration I gave a moment ago of an individual having guaranteed the liability of a friend to a bank. As soon as that liability is paid off, the individual is discharged. Until that liability is paid off there is no discharge of the guarantee. The guarantor is fully liable until the payment has been made. I am suggesting to the Minister that this is the conclusion to be drawn from a reasonable interpretation of the Section to which I made reference.
The Minister has, however, gone into the whole issue of poverty in Canada compared with poverty in the Third World. That raises a very interesting subject for discussion. As a matter of fact, it was with respect to a desire to deal with this issue that I asked this House, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance whether it would be appropriate to refer the entire matter of our foreign aid, both bilateral foreign aid of the kind referred to here or direct foreign aid of the kind administered by CIDA, to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, on which I serve, for a complete analysis and examination.
Of course, we had no such reference. It is very important, now that we begin to deal with the crucial difference between Canadians who are impoverished and those in the rest of the world who are impoverished, to ask ourselves whether it is not in part the responsibility of the wealthy in the poor nations who have gobbled up the national wealth of their own country and come looking to Canadians to bail them out and support them in the style to which they have become accustomed.
At the recent meeting of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund officials in Toronto, there was a congregation of representatives not only from the western industrialized world but from the Third World as well. As a result of that meeting, columnist Barbara Amiel wrote an article in Maclean's magazine making reference to the definition of the new International Economic Order, which was defined by some as a system whereby poor people in the rich countries give assistance to the rich people of the poor countries. She went on to say:
Nothing could bring home the accuracy of the joke better than watching the joint meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank held in Toronto earlier this month, where senior diplomats from some of the poorest countries in the world seemed intent on setting new records for personal and national ostentation. Observers noted wryly that those countries with the largest
delegations, longest stretch limousines and most elegant clothing also scored high on the closest-to-bankrupt index.
It is interesting that Miss Amiel should have noted, as she did, observations which I had made as a consequence of attending, with colleagues from all sides of this House, a meeting in Havana, Cuba in September, 1981 of the IPU. The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council was in attendance with me. He can testify as to the accuracy of the comments I am about to make. It appeared to me and those of us who discussed it that, while we boarded a warm and crowded bus for transportation to and from the convention centre, the representatives of the Third World nations who sat behind us and around us in the conference chamber were picked up in Mercedes limousines, without exception. They were also the best attired and, if I may say so, having regard to the physical condition of some of them, appeared to be the best fed.
I find it ironic that the diplomats representing the poorer nations of the world should come to us and ask for handouts while they treat themselves to the best that money can buy. I would be very impressed indeed to find a representative from the impoverished Third World coming to Canada and saying to us: "As you can see from my attire, we are in need of your help".
All I can say, as matters presently stand, is that I would be more inclined to favour the representations if they had stripped themselves of but a half of their own personal wealth and maybe emptied out some of the Swiss bank accounts they have managed to establish. It is outrageous that we not open our eyes to what is happening around us.
Miss Amiel wrote an article about this. I personally experienced the same feeling of revulsion. I see that the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council is back in the chamber. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), I would like to speak to the House this evening about Bill C-130, an Act to authorize continuing financial assistance to be provided to certain international financial institutions. This legislation will enable the Secretary of State for External Affairs to secure, through parliamentary appropriations, the public funds earmarked for development assistance which Canada contributes through various international financial institutions. Mr. Speaker, this piece of legislation is the result of the ruling made by Madam Speaker on June 12, 1981 on a historic point of order raised about the orderly procedure with respect to certain budget items in the 1981-82 estimates.
Naturally, international financial institutions are a very significant and effective element of Canada's multilateral development assistance program. As far as this legislation is concerned, they include the four regional development banks, namely the Asian Development Bank, the African Development Bank, the InterAmerican Development Bank, the Carribean Development Bank, as well as the concessional funds pertaining to each one, and also the International Fund for Agricultural Development and the Common Fund for Commodities. Canada gives a financial contribution to each of those institutions by underwriting their share capital and/or contributing to their concessional funds. Our payments are made directly or through non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes. The main reason why Canada participates in international financial institutions is that their Third World programs are effective and profitable. Those regional institutions are indeed a particularly appropriate way of promoting regional co-operation and enhancing the self-sufficiency of developing countries. The framework of capital sharing and the nature of financial co-operation among international financial institutions is an excellent example of successful cooperation in the area of development. One of the significant characteristics of our participation in those institutions is the multiplier effect of our dollars thanks to the borrowings of banks on international money markets.
In addition, this complements the other Canadian assistance programs and allows us to diversify our assistance, both geographically and sectorially, and to support the multilateral institutional framework created by these financial institutions. Canada also benefits from the standpoint of its foreign policy and especially of its trade. Our participation is one of the key elements of our relations with less developed countries and reflects the approach of the government to multilateralism and North-South relations. Moreover, Canada's membership in these institutions enables Canadian businesses to bid for certain components of projects financed by these international financial institutions in developing countries, which very often result in major economic benefits for Canada.
Financial Institutions
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this bill is relatively clear and does not call for a lengthy debate. Under clauses 2 and 4, the Governor in Council may amend the schedule, thereby adding thereto or deleting therefrom the names of the financial institutions concerned. Moreover, clause 3 provides financial assistance to these institutions by way of direct payments, demand notes and the purchase of shares. Section 5 states that the sums required for the purposes of the Act must be approved by Parliament and limited to amounts appropriated. Section 6 provides for an interim appropriation valid until presentation of the Main Estimates, next Spring. These sums cover the following investments: the fourth and last payment in respect of the fourth general increase in the capital of the InterAmerican Development Bank, or an amount of $7,290,000, and the fourth payment in respect of the third general increase in the capital of the Caribbean Development Bank, which represents $883,000, as well as the following payments: the first, fourth and last payment in respect of the third reconstitution of the Asian Development Fund for an amount of $56,722,000; the fourth and last payment in respect of the fifth reconstitution by the InterAmerican Development Bank of its Fund for Special Operations for an amount of $18,156,000; a contribution to the Special Development Fund of the Caribbean Development Bank in the amount of $531,000, and finally, the first payment in respect of the third reconstitution of the African Development Fund for an amount of $33,900,000. Except for the payments to the Caribbean Development Bank, all these appropriations will be in the form of notes.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I want to remind the House that some of these allocations are necessary to meet the immediate commitments of Canada to the institutions concerned. This is why I invite my colleagues to act urgently in this regard because if Parliament delays too much or if we are victims of a filibuster by the Opposition so that this bill is not passed before December 31, Canada will not be able to meet its commitment to increase its Development Aid Program to .5 per cent of the GNP by 1985. I know that the Hon. Member for New West-minster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) is very anxious for Canada not only to reach this figure of .5 per cent, but also to exceed it, and I ask for her co-operation and for the co-operation of the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) so that we may meet our international obligations. With this in mind, Mr. Chairman, I hope that the debate will be enlightening, but mostly, I hope it will be brief.

What does the Government think the World Bank is going to do? Is the World Bank in a strong enough position now to avoid the interruption and disruptions in world credit? What do they think of the present situation? How are they going to handle the huge credits we have with Poland, the $1.25 billion that Poland now owes Canada under its grain agreement which is in arrears month after month. How are some of these problems going to be dealt with? What is the role of the World Bank? Why should we give any support to the World Bank at all, or any credit to it? What should be the criteria for loans by the World Bank and other development associations?
Another burning issue of the day about which I get many letters from Canadians is the suggestion we should not have the Inter-American Bank give a loan to Guatemala because of what is happening there. should not provide financing credit for South Africa, and on and on it goes. What is the answer to that? Does the Government take the position that no, Cuba should not have a loan because we do not approve of its system? If the Inter-American Development Bank wants to make a loan to Guatemala, are we taking the position now that we should say to them, through our representative in the Bank, no, you should not make a loan to Guatemala? If that is not our position, why is it not our position? Why do we have a different position? Do we take the position, as I assume we do, that these banks are there to help countries develop, and that these international agencies cannot set themselves up as judges of their own internal system, that they cannot make decisions as to what country should have a loan and what country should not have a loan under some kind of criteria which it is up to the individual to make a decision by? After all, Mr. Speaker, if we cut off relations with countries in this world of whose regimes we do not approve because of their human rights record, or whatever, we would have relations with very few countries in this world. We would not have relations with the U.S.S.R. or Poland or Czechoslovakia, El Salvador, Guatemala, Cuba, and so on. We would be pretty well isolated in the world if that was our policy. This is a Bill which authorizes us over the next few years to provide funds for the development associations and banks, and I have already read them so I will not repeat myself. Do we tell them there are any conditions at all? What conditions do we tell them there should be? The situation of the developing world, Mr. Speaker, is pretty bleak today. The World Bank itself has had to slash its own assistance program by quite a considerable amount. The Third World countries have to import oil and are in what you can only call desperate shape. Their total debt has gone from $96.8 billion in 1973 to $500 billion this year. We know that Canada cannot continue to devote increasing amounts to this area if its own economy does not grow. The principal objective, therefore, of the Canadian Government has to be to get our own economy going again, and our own economic system growing, so we can do more.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I say to you that the Government has lost a great opportunity today. It has had two Bills, Bill C-129 and Bill C-130, which we are now considering. If the Government considers External Affairs and international assistance to be important, and it is one of the few occasions where we have had a chance to even touch on this subject in the House, it should have added to each of those Bills a major statement from the Minister of Finance or Secretary of State for External Affairs, and anyone else in the Government particularly concerned with these issues. The Prime Minister should have been here in this House discussing these issues. Our Prime Minister had these world leaders here a few months ago, but what has he done to follow up on the publicity he was then getting? Mr. Speaker, I hope the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) will be grateful to me, since not only do I agree with much of what he just said, particularly about the shortcomings of the Government, but it was as a result of my request that the Bill is now going to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence so that we can give it the kind of examination that the Government hoped to avoid. It is also for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that I shall not take more than a few minutes tonight. We will have a much better opportunity to discuss this Bill in very great detail when it comes before the Standing Committee.
Like the Hon. Member who just spoke, I was surprised that the Parliamentary Secretary did not have something more to say about the activities of the international financial institutions that this Bill addresses. Perhaps the subject matter of the previous Bill was more familiar to most of us because it concerned the World Bank and IDA, and I think most of us do have a fair bit of knowledge about what they do and about the per capita income of the countries assisted by the IDA. In fact, 80 per cent of those countries have a per capita income of less than $410 a year. However, I do feel, and the Minister should have been aware of this, that there is not as much familiarity, either on the Government side or on the opposition side, with the African Development Fund, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Fund, the Asian Development Bank, even the InterAmerican Development Bank and its fund for special operations, the Caribbean Development Bank and the Special Development Fund, the International Fund for Agricultural Development or the Common Fund for Commodities.
Canada is putting a great deal of money into all these banks and funds, as the Bill indicates, and perhaps it is because the Government has just become so used to introducing measures privately through order in council or estimates and sort of sneaking them in that it does not realize that when it is obliged to come before the House, it is surely expected to give a fairly detailed account and some judgment about the operation of these agencies. Are we to conclude that the Government has not studied the operation of these agencies and that it is simply granting the funds without any study about how they operate or the criteria they use for the granting of loans? Are we to assume it is not interested or that it just simply does not know or think it is important? I really cannot believe that. I know many members of the Department of External Affairs and CIDA are interested, concerned and knowledgeable, but the

November 9, 1982
Financial Institutions
Government seems to have no wish to share that knowledge with us in the House of Commons. Indeed, it appears that it hopes even not to have to go to the Standing Committee on this and thereby deprive us of an opportunity to get the kind of information we want.
So I want to take my few minutes tonight to tell the Parliamentary Secretary in the Minister's absence-and like the Hon. Member who just spoke, I do think it is amazing that he would not have arranged for this Bill to be presented when he was present-to outline some of the main concerns I have so that when the Minister does come to the committee, and of course we will expect the Minister, the leading Minister before the committee, he will have some idea at least of the kind of concerns I have. Some of them have already been expressed by the Hon. Member for St. John's West so I will not repeat those; I will focuss on the other concerns I have.
Now, it has already been said that we cannot be entirely certain about what are the criteria for the granting of loans in these various institutions. In fact, as I understand it, they are fairly specific criteria, which include the IMF as well, and they are criteria that I think we as a country should very seriously re-examine. In a letter I wrote to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) on October 12, 1982, to which I received a reply dated October 28, I asked specifically about the desirability of Canada's supporting the granting by the InterAmerican Development Bank, an institution mentioned in the schedule to this Bill, of a loan to Guatemala. I gave the various reasons that many people give, that the chief purpose of this loan is to finance a rural telephone project. I said in my letter:
It is very questionable that such a telephone system will be serving basic human needs or benefiting low income groups in rural Guatemala. Rural Guatemala is already served by an efficient and cheap telegraph system. It is more likely that such a communication system will be used mostly for the benefit of the government's security forces. The loan should be opposed by Canada for those reasons.
In his reply the Minister said:
As you may know, Canadian policy continues to be that the introduction of political considerations into the decision-making processes of international financial institutions is contrary to their charter provisions and would seriously endanger their viability over the long term, to the detriment of all their members and of the international community as a whole.
In short, he said that there could not be introduced something that he called political considerations. The fact remains, however, that political considerations have in fact been introduced many times, both in the IDB, the InterAmerican Development Bank, and in the IMF whose charter has a similar provision. For example, when the United States pushed the IMF to make a loan of $85 million to El Salvador-which, by the way, all European countries except Italy opposed and which was approved one year after it was introduced with a further $300 million now under consideration-an investigation was carried out in the United States. That was reported in the Toronto Star on September 12, which said that the Dutch Executive Director had remarked that El Salvador's loan application differed from the usual in two respects. I should preface this by saying that most of those loans are to help countries out of balance of payments difficulties. First, this does not establish the existence, let alone the size, of a balance
of payments shortfall. Secondly, it does not contain a staff proposal to the board. Yet this was granted. It was a political loan. They did not even establish the existence of a balance of payments shortfall which was supposed to be the reason for the loan being granted.
There is no doubt that Argentina's request for a loan has strong political implications. The loan request is a direct result of the Falklands war, which in turn, of course, affects the economic situation. Indeed, at this moment in time-and the Hon. Member for St. John's West will be interested to know this-Argentina pays out 100 per cent of its export earnings to finance its foreign debt. One hundred per cent. Clearly there is something very political about that need of Argentina's, and the same, as I have already indicated, is true of El Salvador in its request. I have already suggested that Guatemala does not have in mind the kind of economic considerations that the InterAmerican Development Bank, like the IMF, is supposed to be guided by, according to the Minister's letter.
So we need to have clarification not only of what the guidelines are but some discussions of whether or not Canada should be looking into broader or different guidelines. In that connection, it really came as a great shock to a lot of Canadians to discover that the loan to South Africa recently granted by the IMF of $1.7 billion U.S. is about the same amount as the increase in South Africa's military expenditures for the fiscal year 1981-82. To be more specific, the $689 million U.S. requested from the IMF Compensatory Financing Facility is the largest ever loan request made through that facility, and, coupled with the $394 million U.S. standby credit, approximates the 30 per cent increase in South Africa's defence expenditures for fiscal 1981-82, reaching almost $3 billion.
There are other examples, apart from South Africa, where it is clear that countries are spending massively on military equipment that, I think we all would agree, can be and usually is destabilizing or oppressive or repressive for the region in question. In the case of South Africa, gold devaluation substantially reduced its export earnings, so it asks for and receives a loan from the IMF which is about the same amount as its massive increase in military expenditures.
This is one of the things that I think we should talk about in the committee. If we are genuinely concerned about making international financing institutions viable particularly for the developing countries, surely there should be some direct link between the degree to which they can have a loan or grant and the degree to which they reduce these massive military expenditures that, copying the western world, many Third World countries are undertaking.
That is the first different criteria that the Standing Committee should examine. I hope when the Minister comes before it with his officials, he will already have examined the question pretty closely. It means that there must be some review of the loans granted over the years to the countries that have applied for and secured them from the various financial institutions we
November 9, 1982

are talking about tonight, and also, 1 might add, from the IMF.
The second area at which we might look more closely was hinted at by the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Gamble). And, Mr. Speaker, I never in this world thought that I would agree with him. He spoke about the many countries that are the recipients of bilateral and multilateral grants and loans, and how some of the money does not percolate down to the population but that a great deal seems to be expended by the elite in those countries, rather than by the ordinary people. I am sure that all Members who sit on the Latin American Subcommittee have thought about this; indeed, we could not help but think about it. It causes one to wonder whether the granting of loans should be related in some way to the development of land reform in the recipient country, for example, or should be linked in some way to the efforts made by the recipient country to see to a more equitable distribution of income. Many countries that we visited are certainly trying to do that, and I am not saying it could be done overnight. It should be looked at, however, and like the matter of military expenditures, should be built into our criteria.
The third and final matter that it would be desirable to examine in committee is whether, in a country that is engaging in massive human rights violations-all countries have engaged in some, unfortunately, but some engage in massive human rights violations and Guatemala is a case in point-the money is going to end up causing greater human rights violations and oppression by that particular Government.
This is a difficult question, because we want to help people with basic human needs with development assistance programs and we want these financial institutions to do that. It may be, however, that we should be looking more closely at massive human rights violations as well as at the degree of distribution of income and the growth in military expenditures.
I hope the Minister and his officials will come to the committee prepared to look at the questions that I am sure other Hon. Members will raise tonight, and that they will have thought about them and be able to give a somewhat more satisfactory answer than the one I received in the letter from the Minister. In order to give a more satisfactory answer they will have to study the oepration of the financial institutions and give a report on the financial operation of each and go through some of the more recent and questionable loan applications that have been approved.
Although the IMF is not included in the Bill before us, 1 would be grateful if it could be included in the review that I ask the Minister and the Department to do for the Standing Committee.
The need for full discussion and more information has been pointed out by other Hon. Members. I can only emphasize that if we, as Members of the Canadian House of Commons, are to talk reasonably with our constituents on the long-term benefits of development assistance; if in the face of massive unemployment and lay-offs and the numbers of exhaustees in our ridings, we are going to be understood by them, then we have
Financial Institutions
to make sure we know how the money is being expended. We have to know what the record of the multilateral institution is, along the lines that I have been requesting, and what results have been achieved from loans already granted. I have some knowledge of this and I am sure other Hon. Members have even more, but generally it is not sufficiently known. If we are to do our duty as MPs we must have more information, more illumination.
I agree that long ago we should have had a statement from the Government on its development assistance policy, but apparently that is not going to be forthcoming.
