Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Government nor the officials of CIDA are sufficiently aware of the gravity of the present situation of trying to maintain public support or policies of international development assistance when, as my colleague said in reference to Bill C-129, we are living in extraordinary times in this country.
The Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) dwelled, in his inimitable and illuminating way, on the shortcomings of the Government Ministers in not being present tonight to introduce this legislation. I will not repeat those comments although I certainly agree with them.
We are facing a situation in which there are two competing elements. The first is the domestic crisis of the country. Then there is unemployment, inflation, bankruptcies and fears which were never in the minds of Canadians before. I know of people in Alberta and in Edmonton South who are going bankrupt, just as Hon. Members from Ontario know of similar cases in their constituencies.
It is true that the number of hungry and malnourished people in the world is growing and that there is insufficient health, education and shelter facilities to provide even basic needs for growing numbers of people, now estimated by the World Bank, which is the subject of our discussions tonight, at 800 million people, or one-quarter of humanity.
What is the issue here tonight? What is the issue that this absent and derelict Government does not address? The issue is how we will meet a double responsibility to Canadians and to the dispossessed of the world. How will we do this at a time when we live in extraordinary times which are calling into question the future of international development programs?
It is a tribute to the Progressive Conservative Party and its sense of responsibility that the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) spoke for us on Bill C-129 which dealt with millions of dollars for the World Bank and that the Hon. Member for St. John's West addressed comments on Bill C-130 which is now before us. Both these spokesmen committed

November 9, 1982
Financial Institutions
our Party to supporting these bills, even though the Ministers would not give us the backs, let alone the fronts of their hands.
I do not want to be too hard on the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove). After all, he was here and was asked legitimate questions tonight, especially in Committee of the Whole. He was asked the kinds of questions which Canadians are asking-where is the money going, why should we support the World Bank, why should we support international institutions at this moment when there are such pressing needs at home? I would have thought that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) would have been present. I do not know where he is. It is his Bill. Even with his briefings, I would have thought the Minister of State for Finance would have referred the House, in answer to some of the key questions about where the money for IDA goes, to the World Bank's own report on where it was going. Mr. Clausen, the President of the World Bank, told an international development meeting in Tokyo two weeks ago why he was asking for support. I attended that meeting at which Mr. Clausen used the case of India, the second largest country in the world, with more than 700 million people. With its rate of growth it will probably become the largest country in the world by the year 2020. He said that India had become self-sufficient in food. What does this mean?
I should like to refer to one of the projects of IDA which was paid for by funds contributed by various nations. It was worth S220 million and, according to The World Bank Annual Report 1982:
The project-including construction work on six dams, expansion and remodeling of 217 kilometers of canal systems, and the construction or improvement of 672 kilometers of rural roads-will assist the ongoing development of two major irrigation schemes in Madhya Pradesh state and help increase agricultural production and raise the standard of living of local farmers. Total cost: $439.2 million.
I could quote many examples to show how the money used by the World Bank goes to help people become self-reliant. Why do we want them to become self-reliant? We want them to become self-reliant for humanitarian grounds, so that the world will be a more decent place and so that they can plug into the modern world and trading systems. Also we want them to become self-reliant because there is a mutual interest today between developed and developing countries, between the North and the South. There is a mutual interest in restoring the credit base of Third World countries and in reviving world production to serve as an engine of growth in both the North and the South. This is the basic rationale which the Progressive Conservative Party is supporting.
I hope the CIDA officials who have been monitoring this debate for the last several hours will carry back to their organization some of my comments tonight about the jeopardy in which they themselves are with respect to trying to maintain programs of international development. The Minister was not here to present his own Bill, and the Government refuses to produce a new strategy for international development.
There was a strategy for international development from 1975 to 1980. It contained 21 points. The North-South Institute, which is an independent professional organization, examined all 21 points and reported, at the conclusion of the
five years, that the Government had failed in 16 of the 21 points. As bad as that failure was, the Government does not even produce a strategy for the years 1980 to 1985. No wonder we ask where the Government is going and what is happening in the entire area of international development assistance.
In the course of my remarks tonight I want to indicate-and I should note parenthetically what a rare occasion it is to have the opportunity to debate this subject matter-that we spent a lot of time, as the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) knows, studying very seriously the North-South question in the North-South Task Force. We made many recommendations as well, but I think that in all objectivity he will recognize that they have not been fully implemented or even implemented in the way we thought they should have been. I will be glad to hear his comments in the course of this debate, but he knows that the study was a serious one.
The situation to which Canada is relating is extremely serious, not just on humanitarian grounds, but in connection with our ability to have trading relationships with increasing numbers of people who want to come onstream with selfreliance. He knows, as well as I, that Canada is far behind the United States, Japan and the European community in terms of maintaining trading relationships, with developing countries on both the import and export sides. The trade levels of these three countries which I have just named compared with developing countries are around 25 to 35 per cent, whereas Canada is only at between the 12 and 15 per cent level. We have a long way to go. The North-South issue presents an access for us or a way to increasing trade, the kind of trade which many Canadian businessmen today, such as the 2,500 who have contracts with CIDA, have begun to discover.
How many times do we have to say and underline the fact that it is in our interests as a nation trying to relate to the conditions of interdependence in the modern world for us to maintain our development assistance programs in such a way that we are serving the needs of humanity and the needs of Canada? That is what this issue is all about. That is why this whole debate tonight should have been launched with a major paper by the Government to tell us what is happening with respect to Government policy. How do the officials at CIDA expect to know where they are going to go? I know the question marks and the morale question that CIDA has. I shall come back to CIDA in a few minutes.
Let me talk for a moment about a question that is often raised, that if we have had development assistance for the last 25 years, how come we still have these terrible problems of poverty-that the whole thing does not work? To begin with, in one quarter of a century we have had a lot of declarations, global reports, international conferences, new institutions and new concepts. It would be a whole speech in itself just to relate everything that has gone on. But what it has done for us is to have given us an understanding of how our planet works, how the training, the energy and the environmental interdependent
November 9, 1982

systems of our planet work. Out of that momentum of ideas and activity, we have to ask ourselves, why has the development problem not been solved? Why do the experts keep telling us that 800 million people live in absolute poverty? This figure will rise to one billion by the end of the century. Why do 40,000 infants and small children die every day from malnutrition, disease and inattention in the developing world? The short answer to those questions is that although a great deal has been done to achieve self-reliance in the developing countries, the problem is worsening at a faster rate than the implementation of solutions.
I have had the opportunity of seeing at first hand what the situation is. I have seen areas where food production has tripled with the use of fertilizers and machinery. A few moments ago I referred to India with reference to the IDA appropriation that we put through this House earlier tonight through Bill C-129. India has become self-sufficient in food as a result of this kind of development. I have seen vast cooperative networks for marketing, long rows of new industrial plants, a rising middle-class, clean and well dressed children in schools. I have also seen the bodies of children who died from dysentry. I have seen filthy, stinking slums stretched out as far as the eye can see. I have seen village after village with no electricity, no water and the evening supper heated on a fire of cow dung.
Out of all this, what have I learned? I have learned that the development problem can be solved. The situation is not hopeless. There are enough resources. Economic progress in the bottom sectors of the economy is possible. It is not facts, theories, money or strategies that we are short of; it is the political will. The political will among us in the North must as well be in those leaders in the South. We must understand that it is not just good ethics but it is also good economics to support development partnerships in this modern world.
We have used the word crisis so often in connection with the developing countries, but the word seems to have lost its meaning and serves no one. Yet what other word can be used to describe the mounting number of children who are dying because development programs in their countries have been cut back because the balance of payments have become unmanageable as a result of the higher price developing countries pay for imports of such things as oil together with the lower prices they receive for the export of their commodities. You see, Mr. Speaker, how these questions are interlinked. I have traced it right back to the village level. I have spoken to doctors in Kenya, one of the better off countries in Africa. I have spoken to the flying doctors, as they are called, who go into the bush country. They showed me that children were dying because the development programs were cut back. Why did this happen? Because Kenya reduced its own development program as a result of the cash crisis, the deficit that country accumulated as a result of the higher prices of imports, namely oil and manufactured goods which came from the north, which passed on inflation, whereas the export of Kenya's goods through the manufacturing countries was not subject to inflation and so Kenya got a lesser return. That is the principal reason the gap is widening between the North and the South. That is a question that has to be dealt with.
Financial Institutions
Too often I think we tend to deal with it in negative or pessimistic terms as if the whole thing were terrible. I have said that the problem is out-running the solutions because of the deficits involved. We have made references earlier tonight to the cumulated deficit exceeding $500 billion in the least developed oil-importing countries. What about the progress that has been made? I think we ought to recognize that as a result of the participation of countries like Canada in economic assistance programs which the developing countries of the South have, since all this got started two decades ago, they have doubled their average income, they have halved their rates of infant mortality, and they have almost doubled their average literacy rate-to over 50 per cent. These efforts during the first two development decades have produced some positive results. However, the situation continues to get worse. Even though the situation is worsening, the developing world can at least take credit for the fact that 150 million hectares of new land have gone into production, which is more than all of the present crop land in North America, western Europe and Japan combined. Add to that the doubling of land under irrigation, and we have the reason why only one-tenth the number of people died from famine between 1950 and 1975 as were estimated to have perished from starvation in the much less populaced world of 1875 to 1900.
In these years development has too often been measured by the size of new airports rather than the number of years a child can stay in school. However, the experts-and here again we should recognize the World Bank, the subject of our concern tonight-have led the way in coming to what 1 would call a latter day understanding of the needs and values of community development that if you put money into servicing the needs of people at the village level, that has a far greater economic impact than even some of the mega-projects that have been funded in the name of foreign aid. We are now seeing that the number of years a child can stay in school, the number of projects that will help to fund health, nutrition and education, all of that is not just humanitarian but it has made a major contribution to economic growth.
The fact that the development process is now getting down to the poorest in some areas has given rise to a new ray of hope. Just as this moment of hope arrived, the cost of oil and other manufactured goods for the developing countries went out of sight for them and set back all the development programs, with the result that both the south and the north have fallen into situations of real concern.
I am not going to take the time of the House tonight to trace what Robert McNamara calls the reverse circuits of interdependence by which nations such as Brazil, Mexico and many other developing countries that are so-called better off and have grown the fastest have become in great danger of going bankrupt as a result of their inability to pay the interest or repay capital on increasing amounts of loans which they have acquired. That is one aspect of the situation that the World Bank and the IMF, the International Monetary Fund, have

November 9, 1982
Financial Institutions
had to address, and which they did address at their meetings in Toronto. Some people are quite critical of the World Bank and the IMF, but I am not one of them because I think that both institutions, as the North-South task force recommended, are employing modernization programs and expanding their bases. The World Bank expanded its base, doubling its base of capital, and is now able to secure more money on the commercial markets which it then loans to developing countries, and particularly, to the least developed through the IDA section of the World Bank. It is able to do these things because these institutions are adjusting themselves. That is the fundamental reason these two Bills tonight, which address themselves to a certain expansion of the operating facilities of both CIDA and the inter-regional banks and the World Bank, ought to be supported.
However, there is a certain anomaly here. Those who have watched the debate may be under the impression, with the many figures hurled around, that there is some sort of gigantic expansion taking place in Canada's official development assistance program, but such is certainly not the case. First, we must recall that only a few days ago the Minister of Finance took $245 million out of the forthcoming CIDA budget. The percentage of Canada's official development assistance is now only 0.43 per cent of the gross national product. It is a long way from the 0.5 per cent which the Government has committed by 1985, and it is certainly that much farther from the 0.57 per cent which the North-South task force recommended be achieved by 1985. The enlargement of official development assistance is simply not taking place. There is a certain transfer over to some increase in multilateral assistance, but that will be at the expense of some bilateral programs.
That brings me to some suggestions I want to make to the officials of CIDA and to the Government for their consideration as to how they will maintain a program which is responsive to the needs of the South today and which conjoins the situation in which Canada finds itself, this extraordinary situation wherein all development assistance is questioned. In short, I think it is time we woke up to the fact that the new era in North-South relations has arrived and that it is time to recognize that all the arguments of self-interest, global stability and human justice now converge on the new reality of the interdependent world, namely, that the present global crisis of the international economic system affects both North and South. It is certainly time we gave some recognition to a basic fact that in 1981, three quarters of the total increase in international trade of manufactured goods was represented by imports by developing countries from the North. I say to Your Honour and Hon. Members in the House that we must realize what the statistic is telling us. We are in a recession in the north. We are in a crisis. We are living in extraordinary times. A way out of that crisis is to increase our sales and our exports of goods to that vast section of humanity which is now trying to come onstream called "the developing countries". Here, even in the midst of this crisis, in 1981, and I want to repeat
this, three quarters of the total increase in international trade of manufactured goods was represented by imports by developing countries from the North. That is the signal which ought to encourage us to take some realistic steps, even recognizing that the steps we are taking are less than half of 1 per cent of our gross national product. In the interests of global stability, in the interests of Canada enlarging its own trading relationships in the world, and certainly in the interest of pure human justice, I think we must maintain strong programs and have a strategy for them and an explanation for the Canadian people.
I would propose that CIDA recognize that one of its problems, I would even say its chief problem, is that it has mixed up its motivation as to what it is attempting to do. It is not explaining it. Moreover, its 1,106 projects reach into no fewer than 89 countries on the ground that this provides an entry for Canadian business. We must recognize that Sweden, which is the best aid deliverer in the world, operates in only 20 countries. The development community of Canada is appalled by this misdirection of aid money into so many countries that it loses its effectiveness, and the business community of Canada is simply unimpressed because the figures are far too small to make any kind of imprint in a serious way on Canadian business. Even for all the tied aid that is under so much discussion, the value of it to Canadian business under the bilateral program, according to the last study I saw a couple of years ago, and even in the study which the Government would not release, was that tied aid was equivalent to only 0.23 per cent of our gross national product, so business still is not impressed by the argument.
Rather than carrying on in the way we are, with so many projects in so many countries, I think the time has come when the Government might act quickly with two moves to save CIDA, its reputation and its support. The first of these would be to cut at least in half the number of projects and countries and switch bilateral aid to lines of credit. Under a line of credit, a designated country would be able to use those Canadian goods and services that it really needs, rather than having unwanted projects foisted on it by Canadian officials instructed to move specific Canadian goods, even if the country involved does not need it and it does not fit into its priorities. I have seen many such examples.
If the Government took that first step and moved to lines of credit for most of its bilateral assistance, that would enable a second step to be taken, namely the reduction of the oversized bureaucracy of CIDA. CIDA has more than 1,000 employees in its headquarters here. I guess my friends up there in the gallery will not be happy to hear this, but I think that figure should be cut at least in half, and I hope you do not think I am exaggerating here tonight. If you want to save the support of the Canadian public for international development assistance, you must get rid of that oversized bureaucracy in Hull. The administrative costs of CIDA amounts to $47.73 million-

1 certainly heed your admonition, Mr. Speaker, but I was so intent on communicating my message to these officials, who I know want to take it back to CIDA, that I inadvertently looked up at them in the gallery. They are such handsome fellows and I know they are trying to do a good job, and I will let it go at that.
In any event, before Your Honour kindly interrupted me, I said that the administrative costs of CIDA amount to $47.73 million. This could be cut in half without damaging the proper implementation of aid. By switching bilateral aid to lines of credit, we would eliminate the need for Canadian bureaucrats to trip over themselves in supervising Canadian projects to Third World countries, those countries which have become quite capable of planning and supervising their own affairs.
We do not have a strategy because the Government refuses to give us one. It is no wonder we are asking questions concerning the value of all this. However, I will tell you what the strategy ought to be, Mr. Speaker. Here is the strategy: to go to lines of credit for bilateral assistance, to cut the bureaucracy there, which we would not then need so much, to put more emphasis on the concept of self-reliance in our aid program, to increase our participation in multilateral aid development programs and to provide more matching funds to non-governmental organizations. That is only 7 per cent or 8 per cent of the total CIDA budget now. Dollar for dollar, the non-governmental organizations, of which there are about 100 that are drawing $89 billion of CIDA funds in matching grants, do a better job in getting into community assistance. I have seen it with my own eyes. The non-government organizations of this country are getting short-changed. I would suggest that there is not one party or even one Member of the House who is not in support of the basic recommendations that was made by the North-South task force, that the non-governmental organizations of this country which are doing such a great job should get a better share. Many of those organizations consist of volunteers who go directly into the communities.
1 would like to discuss a major part of our strategy. If CIDA is to be turned around, if international Government assistance is to be turned around, there must be the independent study and analysis which was recommended by our Party in 1979. That study would have lead to a proper strategy which would have taken us through these 20 years, to the end of the century. That independent study would have helped to answer these legitimate questions which are being put on the floor of the House of Commons as to whether aid actually does help the poorest people whom CIDA and we all wish to help.
Another part of the strategy that I will put forward deals with measures to encourage greater private investment in developing countries. We have to encourage Canadian business to enter into joint partnerships and invest in those countries where there is future business waiting, particularly in the energy fields. I would point out very clearly that as part of our strategy as well, no aid whatsoever would go to countries that
Financial Institutions
are themselves conducting military operations in other countries.
These are constructive comments on a positive strategy which I have outlined here today. Since I do not have the responsibility for running a $1.5 billion program-I wish I did-I only hope that members in the Government who have that responsibility will say why it will not lay out a program and strategy that will make some sense and develop some support from all sides of the House.
I want this to be regarded as a serious intervention, Mr. Speaker. I have tried to make my remarks as free of rhetorical exposition as possible, but I think that the time has come to make some serious suggestions with respect to immediate Government policies on the international financial crisis that both of these Bills are trying to address. I would like to put these suggestions before the House in point form so that the Government will take note of them. I hope it will consider these suggestions I wish to make with respect to addressing ourselves to the international crisis of liquidity, to the deficits that are impairing the development of programs and to those international deficits that the World Bank and the IMF in Toronto are trying to address.
I would like to address myself to those deficits that are themselves having an impact, or rebound, on countries such as Canada which are, as part of the North, unable to find the markets and produce goods for those expanding markets because people are unable to become sufficiently self-reliant.
These are some of the steps I wish to suggest. First, there should be urgent action in setting up an international energy financing facility either within or without the World Bank. This would be an energy affiliate of the World Bank, or some such step that has been advocated before, that will not interfere in private investment in energy sources in developing countries. However, that international energy financing facility would help to finance energy investment for the oil importing countries that are prone to these high deficits and that are throwing the international financial community into such disarray.
Second, there should be more interaction with the Governments of these countries requiring them to have regional national energy plans. There should be established an energy nexus with food, so that we may see the relationships much more clearly.
Third, the developing countries should establish, with our co-operation and our export of sufficient food, a reserve of nine million to 10 million tonnes to provide food security as a safety net for those populations that do get caught in crisis that cannot be managed by themselves domestically.
Fourth, we should strengthen the developing countries' capacity to feed themselves through domestic food production expansion programs.
Fifth, we should use effectively the forthcoming GATT meeting. Not much has been said tonight about the forthcoming ministerial meeting of GATT. I believe that the Canadian Government ought to lead the way at that meeting to suggest

November 9, 1982
Financial Institutions
that there ought to be a firm declaration on the standstill of further protectionism, that the GATT nations at the ministers' meeting would employ a standstill on further protectionism. As well, they should finish the Tokyo round of the safeguard clause. We should go for a long-term program for trade liberalization. Those are things to which the ministers should address themselves at the GATT meeting.
Sixth, there should be a doubling of the IMF quotas, just as the capital base of the World Bank has been doubled.
Seventh, there should be a revised policy of conditionality for IMF lending and an automatic provision for refinancing, a consolidation of fund facilities and greater pressure on surplus countries to adjust.
Eighth, a special facility should be established in the IMF for the orderly refinancing of the accumulated debts of the worse-off countries so that they would be recognized as suffering from what I would call debts of duress caused by the failure of the international system to adjust to their needs and problems, which are not caused by internal mismanagement but by the failure of the international financial system to address itself to questions of liquidity that are caused by high imports, low exports and the resulting deficit crisis that infringes upon the lives of people.
Ninth, there should be a new agreement on SDRs to the surplus countries that are unwilling to adjust. They would lose their SDRs to those deficit countries willing to carry the burden.
Tenth, there should be a special concessionary window in the World Bank to supplement IDA Seven. We have talked tonight about the supplement for IDA Six. If the United States maintains its hesitancy to proceed into further growth of international financial institutions, then a supplementary window for IDA Seven, which is almost upon us now, will have to be considered.
Eleventh, there should again be a doubling by us or by the World Bank, which has already doubled its base, with a paid-in contribution of cost-free capital to allow the Bank to function better.
I will conclude with my last point which is that the World Bank should set up a group of thinkers to advise it independently so that the future of international development assistance, the World Bank and international institutions can be modernized and harmonized for the needs of the modern world.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this evening 1 intend to be brief because I know that other Members want to speak on this bill which, at first glance, does not appear to be either complicated or very long, but which is still quite significant.

There are many things I would like to say during this debate. While this Bill is not a very complex one and only provides appropriations for Canadian contributions to some international banks or financial institutions, it does open up
the whole question of Canada's commitment to official development assistance.
Many comments have been made with regard to our commitment. I believe that it is a commitment that is respected throughout the world. There is no time this evening to respond in an intelligent way to all of the questions that have been raised because there are some points which have been made that I believe deserve to be answered.
I am very happy that in this time of recession there seems to be widespread consensus, at least expressed in this Parliament, that Canada should continue to have a strong and sincere commitment to official development assistance, not only because we are human beings and therefore for humanitarian reasons, but because it is to the practical advantage of Canada to develop relationships, whether they are economic, political, social or cultural.
I believe it is important for us to discuss with the Canadian public these issues. I was very happy to hear the comments this evening by the Official Opposition External Affairs critic, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche). They were positive in nature, to the effect that they want Canada to do more. I agree that Canada should do more. Even though these are hard times, there are many people whu would be glad to trade their good times for our hard times.
While the Canadian Government appropriates about $1.5 billion for development assistance, Canadians generally spend a lot of money on things that are less important. For example, we spend about $5.5 billion on liquor and over $6 billion a year on cultural entertainment. To suggest that we have to reduce our activity because of economics is to forget that we have a lot of things we can share with the rest of the world.
I hope the fact that I am not speaking for very long will not be construed as a lack of interest in this issue or with regard to this Bill. I know there are other Members who will want to say a few words. I do not want to delay passage of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly want to say more than a few words on Bill C-130, an Act to authorize continuing financial assistance to be provided to certain international financial institutions.
I have had considerable experience with CIDA and foreign aid, going back to 1975 when the Liberal Government tried to conceal information regarding loans to Cuba. They provided public information that the loans were being made at interest rates of 6 per cent and higher. However, I obtained internal documents which showed that they were concealing the interest rate being charged on loans to Cuba, which was zero per cent and 3 per cent.
Also we are well aware of the low interest loans to Russia for the building of their gas pipeline. This Liberal Government is borrowing money at 17 and 18 per cent and lending it to Russia at 12 per cent. This is a great loss to the Canadian

This, of course, was defeated by the Liberal Members on the committee. The last thing they wanted was an investigation into CIDA. It is too late, Mr. Speaker, I have already made them. I will contratulate you once again on speaking up for the Canadian people instead of following the old Liberal Party line.
I want to speak briefly on the growth of international financial institutions. We have already alluded to the mounting debt problem which is confronting the developing nations.
The World Bank and the other I FIs are merely adding to the problem of mounting Third World debt by ever-expanding lending programs. In fact, World Bank lending to developing nations has increased to about $12 billion a year, which is 12 times what it was in 1968. On top of this already explosive growth, the pending general capital increase for the World Bank will allow lending to double in the 1980s.
The United States' share of this increase will be $8.8 billion, beginning in fiscal year 1982, if the Reagan administration decides to go forward with this initiative as negotiated by the Carter administration. This is something the Government should be studying.
This doubling of the World Bank lending capacity represents about a 2,000 per cent increase in growth within two decades. This is not something we can just slough through this Chamber tonight and into committee without proper debate. The reason I am talking tonight, and I will call it ten o'clock, is that other Members will want to go into this in more detail next week.
A troubling aspect concerning this enormous growth in lending by the 1 FIs is the mounting criticism that the need for ensuring that quality projects are supported is being sacrificed by a desire to achieve increased quantity of lending.
The May 26, 1980 edition of Forbes Magazine contained an article on World Bank President Robert McNamara and his bank. In his article, Forbes states:
Business of the House
Somewhat like a go-go banker who pushes his subordinates to create impressive numbers rather than sound loans, McNamara sets high loan quotas and insists that they be met. It's not that poorer nations don't have plenty of unfilled needs. The question is: How effective are the banks projects in helping generate the income and the foreign exchange needed to pay back their costs?
I go back to 1975. The Liberal Government had negotiated a loan with the Kenyan Government to build a school. The Canadian Government was going to contribute $2 million. Therefore a $2 million cheque was sent to Kenya. When it arrived in Kenya, no one knew what to do with it. They did not want it as they were not ready to build the school. The cheque floated around before finally coming back to North America ending up in a bank in New York, drawing no interest. We can see the importance of having a full-scale debate and allowing Members to discuss the foreign aid problem, how CIDA works, and $2 million cheques floating around the world.
Forbes quotes one World Bank manager as having said:
We're like a Soviet factory. The push is to maximize lending. The quantity-control mechanism means that in May and June (before the end of the fiscal year) the pressures to lend are enormous and a lot of people spend sleepless nights wondering how they can unload projects. Our ability to influence projects in a way that makes sense is completely undermined.
That is the problem we had with CIDA. Of course a lot of this was corrected, but not all of it because unfortunately we were in government only nine months. The Conservative Minister in charge of CIDA did a lot of tightening up with proper accounting controls.
The United States Treasury officials frequently maintain that these criticisms are overstated. It appears to us that there is a growing body of evidence and a growing number of knowledgeable voices stating that in fact these institutions are expanding too rapidly and wasting resources in the process. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 30, 1982, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) and myself made a startling revelation in the House of Commons, namely, that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) would announce the transfer of the Canadian Naval Reserve Headquarters from Halifax on the Atlantic coast to Quebec City on the St. Lawrence River, 1,000 miles inland from international waters. The public reaction was swift, and outside the Minister's own constituency of Langelier in the province of Quebec, virtually unanimous. That is to say, Canadians in the east, centre and west condemned the transfer as both inefficient and ineffective and, more importantly, unfair and unjustified on grounds of national defence and our commitment to NATO. Nonetheless, Mr. Speaker, the transfer was confirmed a few days later by the Minister of National Defence.
What can you expect from a Minister of National Defence who promotes the expenditure of $3 billion on a first-class air fighter interceptor used for coastal protection, then moves the base for the F-18 fighters 500 miles inland to a base at Bagot-ville, Quebec. The economic havoc the closure of Chatham base will wreak in northern New Brunswick might have been justified if our air defence was strengthened. Instead, it was weakened. The Minister's error is now underlined by the fact that United States authorities have expressed serious concern over the shortened range of the F-18 fighter and its reduced refuelling capability.
The brutal fact is that Canada's national defence is in a chaotic state and the minister must bear both the blame and the shame. The National Defence budget was cut by $200 million in the June budget. Then in October, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) announced a further reduction of $230 million. These reductions must be added to the $200 million that will be contributed by the Armed Forces and National Defence personnel to the Government's six and five wage restraint program. That is over $600 million taken away from National Defence expenditures.
Let me consider the state of our national defence program. Can we defend ourselves from attack, and are we honouring our NATO commitments and our international responsibilities, not to mention our duty to our own defence personnel? Here are some practical matters to think about: if a foreign naval force mined Halifax Harbour and approaches, we would have to call upon the United States to provide a mine-sweeping vessel. When our destroyers do make it out of the Halifax Harbour for NATO exercises, they oftei. have to return
because of problems like cracks in their aging boilers. The Sea King helicopters are hardly safe on the ground, let alone on air patrol and must undergo continuous inspection because of mechanical failures.
Let me speak just briefly, Mr. Speaker, about our commitment to NATO. Canada has committed itself to a 3 per cent real growth in NATO expenditures. Instead, we have seen the NATO force diminish in size and capacity over the decade from 1971 to 1981. I want to speak particularly about the effect of cutbacks in defence expenditures and the lack of interest in the matter of national defence as it affects our naval force. Our Navy is left with vessels which are obsolete and outdated. The only hope for the future is the replacement vessel program which centres around the Canadian patrol frigate program. We fear today those cuts in defence expenditures will affect that program and that one ray of hope will be lost to our naval forces. Other elements of the Canadian Forces have suffered harm, Mr. Speaker, but none more than the Navy.
Let me return very briefly to the decision of the Minister of National Defence to transfer the Naval Reserve Headquarters from Halifax to Quebec. His justification was that the Francophone element should have greater participation in the Naval Force, and that the Navy itself should have a greater presence in the province of Quebec. I, for one, sympathize with the legitimate desires of the Francophone population of Canada, but that should not be mixed in with serious considerations of National Defence. At the present moment enlistment is at an all-time low; people are staying in the Armed Forces. So there is no point in transferring the Naval presence to the province of Quebec for an enlistment program which will be nonexistent over the next few years as Canada attempts to get out of this dreadful recession.
What is more important, and what lies at the heart of this subject, is our concern for national defence and our defence forces. We as a nation have to recognize that there are real threats in this world to our country, in fact, to any democratic country. If I may repeat almost 20 years later the words of President John F. Kennedy: Let those who think that there is no threat in this world travel to Berlin and see the situation which exists in that great city. There is indeed, Mr. Speaker, a threat to all democratic nations and our only defence is to have capable Armed Forces, and there is no element more important in our Armed Forces than our naval element.
It is important that the Minister of National Defence not play politics with our Navy and National Defence. It is important that all Parliamentarians stand up and be counted on the issue of national defence and ensure proper financing for our Armed Forces, proper protection for the people of Canada, so that they can live with the assurance that we are taking our place in the nations of the world and that we are concerned with our future and the future generations of
November 9, 1982

Canadians who will be affected by any attempt to destroy our way of life.
Let me conclude on a positive note, Mr. Speaker. It is our sincere hope that the Government will see its way clear to give proper support to the Canadian Armed Forces, particularly to the Canadian Navy, that it will no longer deal with the matter on a political basis, but will recognize the responsibility of Canada and Canadians to national defence.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-GOVERNMENT DECISION ON MOVEMENT OF NAVAL RESERVE HEADQUARTERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER ACT ON ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that such comments as those of the Hon. Member's with respect to the move of the Naval Reserve Headquarters from Halifax to Quebec City have resulted in such a negative perception among some members of the public, such that we are moving virtually the entire Navy up the St. Lawrence. Clearly, nothing could be further from the truth.
For quite some time, and as recently as two years ago, ViceAdmiral Allan, then Maritime Commander, expressed his concern with regard to the low level of Francophone representation in the Navy. Within the Naval Element of the Armed Forces, only 13.8 per cent of the non-commissioned and 9.7 per cent of the officer ranks are Francophones.
The Chief of the Defence Staff agreed with the concerns expressed by the Commander of Maritime Command and gave direction to try to identify ways and locations in which the profile or presence of the Navy could be heightened in the province of Quebec in such a way that Francophones would consider the Navy as a viable career alternative. After careful study several specific recommendations were brought forward by our military advisers. The ultimate aim was to increase the participation of Francophones in the naval service by providing an opportunity for some to live and to serve in a truly Francophone environment, rather than the then current policy of establishing French language units in Halifax, which are little more than Francophone enclaves in an Anglophone world.
To achieve these goals, the Department of National Defence identified the Naval Reserve Headquarters, a small unit within Maritime Command, as a relatively high profile unit that could be moved into Quebec with little or no direct impact on the over-all operations of the naval element. This unit is responsible for the co-ordination and control of the training procedures of the 18 Naval Reserve Units across Canada. It has been located in Hamilton and in Ottawa; before the move to Halifax. The move will not result in any loss of operational efficiency for Maritime Command. If it does in fact result in an improvement in the representation, recruitment and retention of Francophones in the naval service, then it will be deemed a success. Clearly, the initiative is essential if Francophones are to assume their rightful part in Canada's naval service.
I think it is important to point out to you, and it is unfortunate that most media observers missed this point, that the
Adjournment Debate
decision to relocate the Naval Reserve Headquarters to Quebec City was openly endorsed by the Presidents of the Maritime Defence Association of Canada, the Naval Officers' Association of Canada and the Navy League of Canada. These organizations were made aware of this proposal some time ago as a result of a series of visits to reserve units and supporting organizations by Naval officers. Their support of this initiative has been a significant source of encouragement to us. In addition, the Minister informs me that he has received correspondence from former Chief of Defence Staff, Admiral Falls, who also fully endorses this decision.
I hope that the foregoing will place this decision in the appropriate perspective.

subtopic: CHARTER OF RIGHTS-LEGAL COSTS FACED BY ENGLISH SCHOOL APPLICANTS IN QUEBEC

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on August 4, before the House adjourned for the summer, I put the following question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau):
Madam Speaker, since 1978 the federal government has helped citizens and groups finance legal actions against provincial legislation which contravened Sections 93 and 133 of the Constitution. With the new Charter of Rights and the Canada clause, will the government now provide financial assistance to individuals in Quebec who are seeking admittance to English schools this fall under the Canada clause? The Prime Minister understands that, if the Charter is to be effective and meaningful, citizens must have means to enforce these rights in the courts, even to the Supreme Court of Canada.
In August, parents wanted an answer to that question because they were preparing to enroll their children in schools in Quebec. They were not sure whether they could enroll them in English schools under the Canada Clause in the new Charter or whether they would be subject to the provisions of Bill 101. Fortunately, several weeks later the Quebec Superior Court ruled that the Canada Clause prevailed over Bill 101.
Everything looked bright for a few days but soon after that the Quebec Government announced it was going to appeal the case to the Quebec Court of Appeal, and I am sure that after that it will go to the Supreme Court of Canada. My question stands.
In answer to my question the Prime Minister said he could not "give a blanket guarantee" that the Government would advance legal costs in all cases, but that he would see whether something could be done in particular cases. I was not asking that the Government fund all cases of this nature, Mr. Speaker. What I wanted was a statement from the Government that it would fund those cases which would set precedents of interpretation for the Charter of Rights, especially the Canada Clause, and that it would assist those citizens and citizens' groups that would otherwise not go to court.
If we look at the history in Manitoba, where repressive and discriminatory legislation was enacted against Francophones at the turn of the century, but where action was not taken to the Supreme Court until a few years ago by Mr. Forest in that province, we will see that if that action had been taken at the

November 9, 1982
Adjournment Debate
right time in Manitoba, its history would have been very different.
At the turn of the century the Francophone population in that province was 50 per cent, but because of that discriminatory and restrictive legislation the Francophone population declined to the point where it is a very small minority in that province today. Although Mr. Forest won his case with the help of funding from the federal Government, one could say that it was too late. Eighty years had passed since the wrongdoing of the provincial Government of the day. We do not want that to happen again.
If the Charter of Rights is to be meaningful, and if we are to get the interpretations by the courts that are necessary, then the citizens of this country must have the means to go not only before the courts of First instance, but also before the courts of appeal and the Supreme Court. Otherwise, the Charter becomes a meaningless document.
I repeat that I am not asking for assistance in every case. I am asking for assistance in cases which would be precedentsetting.
This past week we had a very successful Liberal convention at which resolution 272 was passed by the plenary session. It read; "Be it resolved that the Federal Government take such measures that may be necessary to fully implement the Canada Clause in the Charter of Rights". That resolution was passed with almost unanimity by the plenary.
Another resolution which was passed by the workshop on the Constitution and language rights, but was not sent on to the plenary because it was not designated as a priority by the workshop-it was a unanimous decision as well and I was present-reads; "Be it resolved that the Government ensure that minority language rights are fully respected since there is sufficient evidence to demonstrate that federal public servants are not complying with the official languages law". That was also fully supported by the convention. These two resolutions were fully supported by the Liberal Party, asking its Government to give support to its citizens, not only in Quebec but the Francophone minority throughout the country.
I pointed out in my question to the Prime Minister that in 1978 the Cabinet adopted a policy to assist legal actions under Section 93 and Section 133, which were the principal ones guaranteeing language rights at that time before the Charter. Certain cases have been funded in Quebec. There were three. One was taken by the Protestant School Board of Greater Montreal, another by the Quebec Home and School Association and another by three small shop owners with respect to signs. The amounts given in those cases averaged between $10,000 and $20,000. Of course Mr. Forest was helped in Manitoba under that policy. Right now there is another citizen in the west who is of the Francophone minority and is being helped. But what is being done there has not been extended, so far, to the enlarged or extended rights given under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
As I said earlier in my remarks, if those rights are to be meaningful to citizens, they must have the means to go to court to have them interpreted in a proper manner. I ask the Government to come out in favour of what the Liberal Party has asked.
[ Translation]

subtopic: CHARTER OF RIGHTS-LEGAL COSTS FACED BY ENGLISH SCHOOL APPLICANTS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to reply to the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) in his mother tongue.

I cannot more fully agree with him.
[ Translation]
Indeed, when the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) asked the same question only a week ago, emphasizing at that time the special situation in which Franco-Ontari-ans find themselves concerning application of Section 23 of the Canada Clause in the case of language minorities in Ontario, I rose in the House to tell him that he had my full support. I was at the workshop at the same time as the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace last Saturday. I was also there Sunday morning when the resolution received unanimous support of the assembly, and I must say, Mr. Speaker, that since then, I have discussed the matter with my colleague, the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan), and that we have assessed the conditions under which some assistance might be granted. I note that many of the views expressed by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace are shared by the Hon. Minister of Justice and myself. With your permission I should like to give you a very brief summary of the conditions under which financial assistance could be extended to certain groups of citizens in relation to the application of Section 23 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, namely the right for official language minorities to attend English schools in Quebec and French schools in other provinces. Mr. Speaker, these conditions would be subject to the following criteria. First, it would have to be a prima facie case with a valid legal basis, supported with serious arguments. The second criteria for offering financial assistance is that the result would have to benefit not an individual, but a group of citizens so that the advantage sought would not be an individual benefit, but a collective one.
A third criterion was mentioned by the Hon. Member in the course of his speech, namely, a case or cases that would set precedents of interpretation for the concepts contained in Section 23 of the Charter, which are still somewhat vague. For instance, the concept and I quote:
When the number warrants-
What does that mean: where the number warrants? Does it mean twenty-two or eighteen parents claiming their right to have a French school, or twelve parents in an isolated community? The concept remains vague, and I think the courts would do well to study the matter and provide a specific answer.
November 9, 1982

Another example, still in the same area, is the concept of educational facilities referred to in Section 23. What is an educational facility? This is another concept that could usefully be examined by the courts. Other criteria that could also be applied include that of non-duplication in a bill on the same subject that might be debated in a provincial legislative assembly. For instance, I do not think it would make sense to take legal action at a time when a province is about to enact the objectives of Section 23 in its own legislature. Another criterion is that such action should basically be concerned with the objectives of Section 23 and should not be used as a delaying tactic or otherwise affect the credibility of the courts.
These are a few criteria which could be considered basic criteria. I can inform you, Mr. Speaker, and 1 am saying this also for the benefit of the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Almond), that I have promised the House to report on the subject, at the request of the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East and especially of the member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), by the end of this year, so that the problems encountered in Manitoba will not recur elsewhere in the years to come. Consequently, I can give the Hon. Member the assurance that his request is being given careful consideration by the government, and by the end of this year, 1 shall be in a position to report to the Hon. Member and to the House on the Government's decision, which I hope will be favourable.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-LETTER CARRIER WALK SERVICES
CANADA POST CORPORATION-LETTER CARRIER WALK SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 17, 1982, I put a question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) who is responsible for the Post Office. My question reads:
In view of the statement earlier this year by the president of the Canada Post Corporation with regard to providing improved postal service, including new letter carrier walks across the country, can the minister advise when these additional letter carrier walks will be provided to rapidly-growing communities such as Elliot Lake, Ontario-
In the Minister's reply he said he would bring the matter to the attention of the President of the Corporation. I hope he has made that representation on my behalf, but so far we have seen no action.
The present situation in Elliot Lake is that of a very rapidly growing community of some 18,000 people. A whole now town is being constructed. Over 1,000 homes have been built in the new town and another 800 or so will be built during the coming year. However, over 1,000 householders have to drive to a postal office and line up at a wicket to receive their mail through the general delivery system. This is most inefficient and it is a very cumbersome manner in which to handle the situation. I am told that some 625 people line up at the wicket
Adjournment Debate
at the Elliot Lake post office each day. This requires a lot of staff to serve the customers.
There are nine full-time letter carriers and one part-time letter carrier. I am told that if their work was re-organized with only one additional half-person year of work, they would be able to provide a full letter carrier walk service to the new town at its present size. All the work has been carried out. The routes have been measured. The preparations have been made but the President of Canada Post just cannot get around to designating one additional half-person year of work to carry this out.
The president just raised the price of postage by another two cents and earlier this year there was a massive increase. At that time he referred to better service, better morale among the postal workers and more productivity, but he certainly has not achieved these goals as far as the patrons in Elliot Lake are concerned, and certainly not in that part of the community which is growing very rapidly.
I would like to suggest to the Parliamentary Secretary, who is responding for the Minister, that these recommendations be taken into account in view of his statements earlier this year about improved service, increased postal costs and so on, because the present system is very costly to patrons; to some 600 or 700 people who must get into their cars each day and drive several miles to the Post Office to line up at the wicket, all for the sake of one half man-year of work. It must be the most inefficient system for the Post Office and the people working there. It is certainly non-productive for the postal workers, simply because the Government cannot get around to providing this additional half person year of work so that the letter carrier walk service could be put into place.
It seems to me that if the President of Canada Post wants to stand and make these glowing speeches about how he will improve the postal service, he should look at places like Elliot Lake instead of sitting in his ivory tower out at Confederation Heights designing grand schemes. He should get busy and provide the additional finances for the service to be improved. Certainly, the present system is a shame, a disgrace and is totally unacceptable. I simply hope that the Post Office, the President of Canada Post Corporation and the Government will take some action on this situation and correct it immediately.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Berger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-LETTER CARRIER WALK SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) for his additional comments on this subject.
I am pleased to report that Canada Post Corporation is aware of the need for expanding letter carrier service in growing communities across Canada, such as Elliot Lake, and is taking action on the matter. A few months ago the President of the Corporation announced that 75,600 new homes and businesses across Canada would be served by 170 additional letter carriers. Delivery to most of these addresses became

effective on April 1, but it seems that this has not yet benefited Elliott Lake. This particular expansion represented a $5.5 million investment in provision of faster and more accessible mail services.
Another matter which perhaps may be more relevant to Elliott Lake, according to the notes I have been given, is a collective agreement with the Letter Carriers Union which provides for productivity sharing on mail routes. The increased productivity will free up a substantial number of new person years which will be allocated to the expansion of letter carrier services. This agreement applies to grade seven staff offices across the country. Elliott Lake has such an office, and I am told could benefit from the agreement early next year. 1 would
therefore hope that the Hon. Member's wait, and that of his constituents, will not continue much longer.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are indicating the time which has been allotted to me is coming to an end. I would just like to undertake to follow up on the question of the Hon. Member and on the information which I have been given, and to do anything I can to help him see a quick resolution to this problem.
